en: The Essential Collection of the Buddhas, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha, staying among the mango groves in that district.

To the north of the land there is a mountain named Indrasailaguha—Indraśailaguha in the language of Jin (Chinese)—meaning "The Cave of Indra’s Tree. There, [the Buddha] was together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, numbering five thousand;

and twenty thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive and possessed the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Their body, speech, and mind were concentrated, and they comprehensively mastered the three periods of time. Walking alone through the triple world, they transformed and enlightened sentient beings, providing medicine according to their ailments so that each might find their proper place.
Among them were Mañjuśrī, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and others. Furthermore, there were eighty-four thousand devas, all of whom were resolved upon the path of the Buddha.

At that time, the fourfold assembly each went to visit the Buddha; although they wished to listen to the sutras, they were unable to apply themselves with single-minded devotion and grew weary of the Dharma being preached. Each was preoccupied with many worldly pursuits, chasing after the five turbidities as their primary occupation.
The Buddha thought to himself:

"The multitude are weary of and find fault with the teachings I have proclaimed; they are unwilling to come again to inquire and receive the words of the Dharma. Not seeing the Tathāgata and not hearing the true scriptures, these words do not enter their minds or ears; their hearts do not contemplate them, and thus they are unable to practice and establish them."
The Buddha thought to himself:

"I wish to manifest a semblance of dwelling in seclusion, yet without revealing my physical form, to go to the buddha-fields of other directions and, together with all the Buddhas, proclaim and expound the Essential Compendium of the Buddhas."
The Buddha again surveyed them: "Where do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, assemble?

He immediately beheld the eastern direction, eighty-four thousand *koṭis* of Buddha-worlds away; that land was named Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*), and its Buddha was named Heavenly King (*Devarāja*) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who was currently preaching the Dharma, and there the Buddhas were assembled.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"The Tathāgata shall enter the old chamber at Indrasailaguha to sit in meditation for three months. Should any devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans come to him, you must explain the matter to them and prevent them from entering the chamber."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

"The Great Sage bestows his grace; there are honored ones, lofty and majestic, with spirits and wonders like those of the devas. Their majesty penetrates all things, their physical forms are subtle and wondrous, and their mental intentions are invisible. As they come and go and move about, one cannot guard against them."
Since they are weak and inferior, lacking the power of the *ṛddhipāda* and divested of the armor of great virtue, their miraculous transformations do not equal those of Maudgalyāyana.

As for Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Tathāgata has praised him as foremost in the *ṛddhipāda*; he flies to the ten directions without obstruction, and alone is worthy of being entrusted with the protection of future affairs.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not speak such words! The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, does not require protection from others."

Now the Buddha observes the heavens and the world—including all Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, humans, and asuras—and sees that none are able to exert power or cause any movement in what the Tathāgata, the Unsurpassed and Truly Realized One, has established.
"You should remain silent; the Tathāgata is able to protect himself within the assembly and requires no guards.
Furthermore, Ānanda!

If there should come to you any male or female destroyers, or perfumed men or women, or gods, nāgas, spirits, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans, while the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, is sitting in meditation, you should preach this teaching of the Dharma to them: "

"The Dharma is difficult to encounter, and its definitive meaning is likewise so; a human body is difficult to obtain, and the path of the sutras is rare. A Tathāgata appears in the world only once in vast eons, and to be able to believe in the scriptures proclaimed by the Tathāgata, to leave the household life for the sake of the Way, to meet virtuous teachers and friends, and to be able to receive their instructions with diligence and joyful devotion—these too are difficult to find."
Furthermore, to encounter a monk learned in the scriptures who preaches the pure Dharma is impossible to obtain; yet one’s mind delights in giving.
To meet with the Benefactors (the Sangha) and bestow upon them offerings, receiving their ability to bring purification to completion—this too is difficult to encounter.

Even if one were filial and obedient, repaying kindness with gratitude, and furthermore diligent in study, upholding the sutras and precepts without fail even unto death, such a person would still be difficult to encounter.

Yet, if there should be someone who takes pity on sentient beings and resolves to attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of enlightenment—and having just resolved their mind, is immediately able to follow and accord with the Buddha’s teachings, perfecting the bodhisattva path—that is the most difficult of all.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"When the Tathāgata is in secluded meditation, the fourfold assembly, as well as devas, nāgas, spirits, asuras, humans, and non-humans, will come to you desiring to hear the Dharma. You should proclaim such teachings of the Dharma for them."
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"You shall receive the Buddha’s teaching and proclaim it thus:

'The Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, employs countless skillful means to transform people according to the times, causing them to abandon what is non-Dharma, confusion, and false views; you all, receiving this command, shall cultivate the truly correct teaching.'"
“Ānanda! In this regard, what is called wrong view? It refers to performing prostrations to the deceptive arts of others;

following various heavens and serving ghosts and spirits; worshipping withered bones, decaying wood, mountains, trees, rivers, streams, springs, rocks, and earth deities; the heavens and earth, the sun and moon, the directions of east, west, south, north, the Big Dipper, and the local deity; or serving various extraordinary *piśācas* such as pythons, snakes, birds, beasts, elk, deer, and dragons—this is called wrong view.”
"Furthermore, Ānanda! To calculate a self, to be attached to a person or a life-span, and to hold views of annihilationism or eternalism—this is called wrong view.

To state the essentials, I shall further explain for you what constitutes subtle wrong view: if sons or daughters of good family give rise to deluded thoughts, desiring to attain the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, or further desiring that upon attaining Buddhahood they should enter parinirvāṇa—all such things are entirely wrong views."
"Furthermore, Ānanda! When the Tathāgata, the Arhat, is in seclusion, he should explain such essential teachings as these:

'You who are students must always aspire to the meaning of the Dharma and delight in the joy of the Dharma; take the Dharma as supreme, practice purity with mindfulness, take pleasure in sincere faith and much rejoicing, and be modest, respectful, diligent, and filled with a sense of awe and trepidation.'"

Abiding within the triple world, they attain liberation without doubt; they practice the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Wherever they travel, they always act in accordance with the proper time; they are patient, harmonious, gentle, humble, and submissive in spirit. They seek only the ultimate meaning and do not grasp at ornate embellishments; they seek only wisdom and do not grasp at consciousness or attachment; they seek only the sublime sutras and do not grasp at flowery rhetoric; they seek only the True Dharma and do not rely on persons.
He instructed them to practice the profound and wondrous patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).

What is called "liberation" refers to the three gates of liberation: diligently honoring the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) without reckoning a self; practicing signlessness (*animitta*) by casting away all expectations; and practicing wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) by eliminating all vows.
"You should explain the twelve links of dependent origination to sentient beings:
all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; if there were no causes and conditions, they would neither arise nor cease."
One should carefully and thoroughly contemplate the arising of the twelve links of dependent origination, examine its root source, and practice accordingly;
for if one does not carefully contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, such difficulties will arise.
How should one contemplate this?

Ānanda, you should know that the twelve links of dependent origination are entirely unarisen. That which is unarisen is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). If one does not give rise to such thoughts, this is the profound and accurate contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
"One should further distinguish the noble and correct practice and preach the Dharma for the multitude.
What is called the Noble Truth?
It is the sincerity and faithfulness of one's conduct."
Regarding these Noble Truths: if one listens to and contemplates the Noble Truths with the mind, there is neither falsehood nor deception;
because there is neither falsehood nor deception, they are therefore called the Noble Truths.

The meaning of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is that which is sincere and trustworthy, yet non-arising. That ultimate truth is truly authentic; it is the truth of detachment from desire, the truth of faith and understanding, the truth beyond verbal expression, the truth of non-action, the truth of not creating suffering, the truth of non-existence, and the truth of neither correspondence nor non-correspondence, neither elevation nor depression—it is the Single Truth. It is the truth of no transgression and the truth of no extinction; it is the unconditioned truth (*asaṃskṛta-satya*).
"Suppose, Ānanda! One understands that all phenomena neither arise nor cease, that they are entirely without abiding and no different from sentient beings—this is called the Noble Truth."

For this reason, the Tathāgata has taught this Dharma: when a wise disciple practices the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) with the desire to understand wisdom so that suffering does not arise and reaches the state of non-arising, this is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

If one encounters affliction and dwells in suffering, yet does not cultivate conditioned formations and severs the causal conditions—such that the causal conditions are already severed—this is called abandoning the Truth of Origination.
If one can eternally extinguish all suffering so that it never arises again, this is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
What is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*)?

If one cultivates the meaning of the path such that one does not engage in dualistic karma, and if wholesome and unwholesome dharmas enter into a single category of illumination while seeking such a way, this is then named the Three Gates of Liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*).
All past Buddhas and their disciples have, by means of this path, reached the state of non-attainment and entered parinirvāṇa;
this is called the Eightfold Noble Path: first, right view; second, right mindfulness.
Third is right speech;
fourth is right action;
fifth is right livelihood.
Sixth is right effort; seventh is right mindfulness;
eighth is right concentration.
By means of this protection of the mind, one speaks of equality; when the nature is equal, one harbors no delusive thoughts regarding all phenomena—this is called returning to the direct path.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

When the Dharma is taught in this manner, you should diligently apply yourselves to the four foundations of mindfulness, proclaiming and explaining the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment for the sake of the assembled multitude, so as to establish the teachings of the Dharma."
What is meant by "those thirty-seven factors"?
If one abides in accordance with the ultimate meaning, all things are spontaneously realized as being merely conventional designations of words.
If one regards words as equal [to reality], the Tathāgata establishes all dharmas by means of them.
These syllables are also naturally empty, neither arising nor perishing.
Whether one speaks of them or does not speak of them, they are equal; they neither increase nor decrease. Thus, because the syllables are equal, they are [themselves] equal.
"Suppose, Ānanda, that bhikṣus understand syllables as the meanings that accord with the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma).
Furthermore, Ānanda..."
When the Tathāgata is in Yan, if there should come gods, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, humans, or non-humans, he shall preach for them the equality of the three periods of time.
What are these three?
That which has passed away is already extinguished; that which is yet to come does not manifest; and that which is present has no abiding. To fall into such inversions is itself primordially pure.

All phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise entirely empty; they do not exist in the three periods of time, nor do they have any abiding place. The past is empty, the future is empty, and the present is also empty. They are like the emptiness of emptiness itself, and even the absence of emptiness is empty. Just as the three periods of time are empty, so too is the person (*pudgala*) empty.

The emptiness of the three periods of time is called equanimity; entering into this single principle, there is no multiplicity. If one preaches the Dharma in this way, it can eliminate the three realms and thus bring peace.
“What is meant by being able to eliminate the three realms?

If there is a bhikṣu who, at the appropriate time, reflects upon and observes them—the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—he realizes that they are born of mental conception; and as for that mental conception itself, it too is non-existent.”

Having realized that the three realms are non-existent, they conceive thoughts where there is no thought; they are neither diligent nor indolent, have nothing established, and make no vows. They neither think nor reflect, having relinquished all mental conceptions, and thus attain the three gates of liberation. With earnest and focused diligence, they cultivate clear realization, upholding the three gates of liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
What are the three gates of liberation?

To attain clear realization while not abandoning equanimity; to be unimpeded regarding all phenomena, neither acting nor refraining from action; and to know that all phenomena must ultimately reach exhaustion, yet without entering into meditative absorption or falling into mental decline, and without calculating whether there is "one" or "many"—these are the three gates of liberation through which one attains clear realization.
"Furthermore, Ānanda! You should preach the Dharma for them so that they may transcend the five aggregates. What are these five? "
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these are the five aggregates (*skandhas*).
To accept these is to possess the heavy burden of the aggregates; by not accepting them, one is without aggregates.
If one practices while dwelling in seclusion, one should cultivate this contemplation.

The Tathāgata has constantly taught that form is like a mass of foam, sensation is like a bubble, perception is like a mirage, mental formations are like a plantain tree, and consciousness is like an illusion. The Buddha’s radiance surpasses the sun, and his wisdom exceeds the void; he personally proclaimed these instructions to practitioners, saying: "You should cultivate this contemplation."

Regarding the meanings expounded by the Tathāgata that are accessible to entry, I do not understand them and thus do not immediately seek clarification: the desire realm is like a mass of foam and is likewise empty; the form realm is also non-existent, and the formless realm has no location. One does not cling to the three realms; for one who does not rely upon them, there is no place of abiding. A mass of foam is without self, without person, and without life-span. For this reason, all dharmas are devoid of persons or sentient beings, being entirely like masses of foam, bubbles, mirages, and plantain trees.

Consciousness is like an illusion or a transformation and is likewise empty; it does not cling to the three realms. If one wanders through all phenomena without clinging to the three realms, there is no location and thus nothing to rely upon. That which is illusory and transformative no longer dwells within the notions of self, person, life, or soul; that which realizes reality likewise lacks the basis for self, person, life, or soul. When one contemplates the five aggregates in this way as having no location, then the five aggregates do not exist.
"Furthermore, Ānanda! You should further preach the Dharma, analyzing and eliminating the six internal and external bases (āyatana), and analyze them in full detail.
What are the internal and external six bases?
The Tathāgata has always taught that the self is empty. Why is this?
Because all things are fundamentally pure;
thus, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also empty, being fundamentally pure and devoid of a self.
If, by nature, they were pure, empty, and devoid of the sense bases (*āyatana*), then there would be no spheres of form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, or mental phenomena (*dharma*).
Furthermore, if there were no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, there would be no consciousness arising from causes and conditions, nor any of the six internal or external sense bases.
What are the six external sense bases?

Regarding all phenomena, there is nothing to be grasped and nothing to be relinquished. The various external sense bases arise from conceptualization; if one does not cultivate these sense bases, they have no locus.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“When the Tathāgata is in quiet seclusion, if anyone comes, you should explain the meaning of such Dharma for them.
The Buddha establishes his majestic spiritual power to manifest his transformations; if there are those who are suitable vessels and destined for deliverance, they shall all hear this Dharma.”
The rest of the assembly neither saw nor heard anything; they beheld only the Buddha remaining silent, with no words issuing from his mouth.

When this Dharma was taught, five thousand bhikṣus attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of mind; forty-two thousand devaputras were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; three hundred bhikṣuṇīs attained arhatship; and seven thousand people became free from craving and desire.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished instructing Ānanda, he further addressed him:
"Go to the stone chamber and prepare a seat for the Tathāgata; use only kusha grass, for the Tathāgata shall sit upon it and dwell there in seclusion for three months."
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “One should provide beds and mats and have them spread with fine, soft materials; why use straw?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Stop! Stop! All the Buddhas of the past—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—all used bundles of kusha grass as their seats; they did not consider soft, ornate, or multi-layered cushions to be excellent or pleasing. To practice and accord with the Dharma of the Path is what constitutes true great peace."
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately rose from his seat, left the assembly, and went outside to seek grass.
At that moment, countless hundreds of thousands of billions of devas each took soft, exquisite celestial grass and placed it before Ānanda.
Ānanda immediately took it and went to the stone chamber, where he prepared a seat of *kuśa* grass for the Buddha.

Once the preparation was complete, at that very moment, countless hundreds of thousands of billions of devas each took celestial robes and spread them upon the grass. The number of robes spread there was so vast that even if they were laid across the entire world, they could not have contained them all;
yet through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the spread robes were transformed to be only four inches high.

The Buddha rose from his seat and entered the stone chamber beneath the *tāla* tree; immeasurable musical instruments played spontaneously without being struck, and the heavens rained down various flowers that accumulated knee-deep throughout the great trichiliocosm. The Buddha then sat in peaceful meditation, entering the samādhi of right reception, and transformed the stone chamber so that it became entirely like crystal. All sentient beings within the three thousandfold world-system whose roots of virtue were pure and mature beheld the Tathāgata sitting within the stone chamber, just as one sees the reflection of one’s own face in a clear mirror.

The Buddha emanated hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light from his right palm; these rays shone universally throughout the trichiliocosm, completely eclipsing the light of the sun and moon.

At that time, all sentient beings were freed from lust, anger, and delusion; they harbored no self-importance, arrogance, envy, or jealousy, nor did they suffer the afflictions of weariness or contention. With hearts of loving-kindness directed toward one another, they regarded each other as fathers and mothers, elder and younger brothers, sons, or their own bodies—indistinguishable in their equality.
The World-Honored One’s samādhi is such that its practice is eternally settled, without abiding and without karma; it is naturally like space, acting without deluded thought.

At that moment, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and within the Buddha-land, the majestic spiritual power and miraculous transformations of the Buddha were manifested. Twenty-two thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path. Each took celestial flowers and scattered them over the stone chamber as an offering to the Buddha; after circumambulating the chamber three times, they suddenly vanished.

The flowers scattered by the devas completely covered the mountains and valleys, transforming them into Buddhist temples; their fragrance pervaded the entire trichiliocosm, such that there was no one who did not inhale its scent.
The Buddha then manifested a transformation body and proceeded to the place of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Tianwang (Heaven-King), arriving at the world of Universal Radiance (Puguang).

At that time, the Buddhas of the lands throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, because the sentient beings of the five turbid worlds were difficult to transform, all manifested their arrival at the abode of the Buddha Heavenly King. They were just like the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Śākyamuni; for in those lands, lust, anger, and delusion were rampant, and beings were arrogant, conceited, rebellious, and unfilial, full of flattery and evil thoughts, with their wills set on inferior attainments.

Why is this? Because the sentient beings of their own land do not go to see the Buddha and are unwilling to receive his teachings; even when they have heard them, they do not listen, do not enter into them, do not contemplate them, and do not practice them accordingly.

For this reason, the Buddhas, through their skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), remain seated in their pleasure chambers, yet further manifest transformed bodies to go to the realm of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*) where they approach the Buddha Heavenly King (*Devarāja*) to preach and analyze the *Sūtra of the Essential Collection of All Buddhas*.
"What is meant by the 'Essential Compendium of the Buddhas' (Buddhāvadāna-samuccaya)?

It refers to the various practices recorded by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, which are fully prepared for the sake of non-attachment, and which further advance toward the ultimate finality; because they manifest compassion and love for sentient beings, this is the meaning of the scripture titled 'The Essential Compendium of the Buddhas.'"

After the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, has entered parinirvāṇa, he shall remove the veils for the sake of sentient beings. The Great Sages, the Buddhas, are the Lords of Dharma; their virtue exceeds Mount Sumeru, their wisdom surpasses the rivers and seas, and their Way transcends empty space—beyond all comparison. Yet, because all foolish people are indolent, negligent, and do not comply with the teachings of the Dharma, they receive these scriptures [only to disregard them].
Why do they become indolent and deluded, bound by the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-nīvaraṇa*), and fail to escape the three miserable destinies?
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perceive this meaning, they have compiled this essential collection of the Dharma.
"At that time, in that world of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā), incalculable and countless Buddhas all gathered together in that land.
For what reason is it called 'Universal Radiance'? "

That land is pure and true, and even the names of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not exist there; it is entirely filled with bodhisattvas. Each of those bodhisattvas possesses their own golden radiance, and their bodies are adorned with the primary and secondary marks of excellence. Their light shines forth universally, pervading everywhere without exception; therefore, it is called "Universal Radiance."
"What is meant by 'The Essential Collection of All Buddhas'?
It is the honoring and revering of all dharmas according to ultimate truth.
What are meant by 'all dharmas'?"
What is meant by "veneration"?
What is meant by "following"?
All dharmas are but a single dharma; these dharmas are neither existent dharmas nor non-existent dharmas, and they cannot be described in words.

Why is this so? Because that which is without dharma is neither produced nor arises; yet the teaching of the Dharma is spoken for them, though it does not endure for long, being merely a provisional expression.

There are the six internal sense bases and likewise the six external sense bases; the five aggregates, the various elements, and the sense bases—these are called "all that exists," which are merely conventional designations used to differentiate words and phrases.

When all phenomena are observed according to the True Reality, there are no five aggregates, no four bases, and no sense-fields; there is neither annihilation nor permanence, and nothing that is solid. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are ineffable.

All dharmas are fundamentally pure and thus empty; they possess no names, and that which is spoken of as "life" likewise does not exist. All dharmas and their designations are naturally and entirely non-existent; this is the essential compendium of all Buddhas.

"What is meant by 'veneration'? It means venerating detachment, wherein nothing at all arises; venerating desirelessness, venerating the True Reality (*satya*), and venerating the absence of origin. One venerates the Dharma-realm and venerates the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). All phenomena are entirely empty; one venerates this True Reality. All phenomena abide nowhere, are not practiced, and involve neither action nor non-action. Regarding dignified conduct and etiquette, one does not grasp at the future."

Being without "mine" and without any karma that is received, there is neither sovereign nor clothing; it cannot be seen, for being ultimately exhausted, it cannot be exhausted—this is expressed through provisional words.

That which is inexhaustible is without arising; it is fundamentally pure, meaning that when the will is tranquil, there is likewise no arising. Having abandoned both arising and non-arising, that which is venerated is neither sound nor silence; it cannot fall away, nor is there anyone who retreats. Apart from all forms of encouragement and assistance, it has neither bottom nor lack of bottom; it neither arises nor is born. It proclaims equality and is free from conceptualization; it is neither near nor far, and it leaves no tracks. Therefore, it is called "venerated."

"That which is venerated is called entering the city of Dharma. All dharmas are merely provisional designations; they neither come nor go, neither are attained nor unattained. There is no departing and no returning; they are neither correct nor deviant, neither heard nor seen, neither thought nor known, neither fearful nor terrified, neither loving nor abiding, neither quiescent nor non-quiescent, neither coarse nor subtle, neither long nor short, neither middle nor other, neither arriving nor hidden. They do not obtain causes and conditions, are neither secure nor perilous; they are entirely incomprehensible and have no course of action. There is nothing to be raised or abolished, nor anything to be removed. One does not cause them to arise, does not nourish them, and does not sleep upon them; there is no reflection, no conceptualization, no penetration, and no recollection."

It is without limits or boundaries; its thoughts are immeasurable. It has nothing to guard and nothing to protect; it summons nothing forth. It does not cross to the other shore, nor is it in a place, nor is it not in a place. It is neither annihilated nor eternal; it is neither lost nor gained. It is without past, future, or present; it is without wisdom and without non-wisdom. It is neither many nor few; it is without sound and without speech. It does not enter into anything; it is without fear and without characters, nor does it enter into words.
It is unmoving and unshakable; neither distant nor near; without ritual propriety and without its absence; it does not seek renown, nor does it possess a self.

It is without person or life-span; it neither observes precepts nor violates them; it is neither patient nor contentious; it is neither diligent nor indolent; it is neither that which can be attained nor that which is non-existent; it is neither pure nor impure; it is neither empty nor non-empty; it is neither body nor bodiless; it does not discourse on names or titles, being equal to empty space itself.

There is no completion and no non-completion; there is no teaching and no transforming; there is no aspiration and no detachment; there is no doing and no non-doing. Because there is no transgression, there is also no eradication of sin; there is no thought and no non-thought; there is no movement and no relinquishing. One gives and yet does not receive it; from the beginning, one does not bestow it. There is no disciplining and no tranquility; there is no extinction and no inequality. One does not cause things to be reduced to ashes; one is neither dust nor detached from dust. One does not fall and does not descend; one is neither defiled nor undefiled. There is no forgetting and no recollecting; likewise, there is neither sorrow nor grief.

Without thought and without non-thought, without response and without non-response; neither dual nor singular; not wandering and not abiding; not on this shore and not on the other shore; not there and not here; not on the bank and not on dry land; without bottom and without middle; not dwelling in crossing; no one who can cross; without moving traces and without aspiration; non-retrogression; neither conjunction nor meeting; neither severed nor destroyed; not reuniting; not comparable; neither attached nor detached; neither grasping nor non-grasping; neither empty nor non-empty; a radiance without bottom; having no love for life; without person and without teaching; always preaching the relinquishing of all locations—this is the entry into the City of Dharma.

Those who do not enter [the realm of signs] are invested with the title of "Bodhisattva"; they preach the Dharma of non-attachment and do not perceive a place of abiding. This is called "veneration," and it is the essential compendium of the Buddhas.
What is meant by "following"?

All phenomena are eternally abiding within the Dharma-realm; those who are able to practice such a Dharma are said to be "in accord. What is meant by "Dharma"? That which is called Dharma does not involve recollecting phenomena, nor does it involve removal or destruction.

It is without expectation, yet there is no lack of expectation; even if there is no expectation, there is also no thought of retribution. If one does not think of retribution, then all delusive thoughts are eliminated. One creates neither much nor little; one neither arises nor ceases. One does not recollect the past, does not imagine the future, and does not dwell in the present. A practitioner who acts in this way is equal toward the three periods of time and is beyond verbal expression. Because they do not abide [in anything], they lead sentient beings [to liberation]; this is what is called "Dharma."

"Therefore, the Tathāgata proclaims this teaching: whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the characteristics of reality remain as they were; the dharma-realm is likewise so. That which abides as the dharma-realm is the quiescence of the dharma-realm."
For what reason is it called "Dharma"?
That which attains tranquility is illustrated by means of purity; for this reason, it is said that "all dharmas are tranquil.
What is meant by "lack of purity"?

I reckon that what I call "my own body" arises from the causal conditions of various views, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and speech; it depends upon consciousness (*vijñāna*). This refers to what is designated by names, what the mind contemplates, measures, and examines from beginning to end, and what the intellect focuses upon. I shall accept these five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the various sense bases, and I shall encourage and transform those within the three realms. By abandoning lust, anger, and delusion, I shall practice the Way of the Buddha, realize the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*), and attain the fruits of the path: the stage of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and the state of an Arhat.

I shall contemplate and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, up to the eightfold path; these thirty-seven factors of enlightenment illuminate the four truths and extinguish all afflictions—this is the stage of the śrāvaka, which is called "impure."
"In this regard, what is meant by 'tranquility'? It refers to those who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle and resolve their great mind, saying:

'I shall attain Buddhahood and diligently seek the wisdom of the Way. Regarding these practices, I shall practice giving and abandon stinginess and greed, bestowing the wealth of the Dharma; I shall purify my precepts and sever all deficiencies; I shall guard my conduct with vigilance and establish patience; I shall cut away anger and cultivate gentleness; I shall cultivate diligence to cast off the defilement of indolence; I shall follow the power of effort and dwell in seclusion to cultivate meditative absorption (*samādhi*); I shall act as a teacher to transform others and regain a unified mind; arising from samādhi, I shall contemplate the *prajñāpāramitā* and carry out its meaning; through the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*), I shall enlighten sentient beings in the pursuit of the Buddha-way.'"

"All Buddhas are born from Prajñā; having attained the Buddha-way and subdued the various Māras, they then turn the wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings. By means of the Buddha’s unconditioned state, they bring about parinirvāṇa; they perfect the Buddha-wisdom and study all the works of the Buddhas. They proclaim the activities of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the roots of all powers, and the four fearlessnesses, possessing analytical eloquence and extensive mastery."
Regarding the establishment taught by the Bodhisattva, one should attend to its entry, exit, advancement, and withdrawal; this constitutes the locus.
As for all expectations, conceptions, and whatever is grasped or received—how could these ever be put into practice?
There is no such dharma; this is called the pure, virtuous, and tranquil non-existence.
That which is tranquil is what is called the Dharma, and this is named the Essential Collection of All Buddhas.
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, that which is called 'The Essential Assembly of All Buddhas' refers to the teachings for those who have first resolved to attain the Bodhisattva mind.
What is meant by 'those who have first resolved to attain the Bodhisattva mind'? "
This means there is no arising from anything. Why is this?
Because within all minds, there is no mind.

That which is mindless is without arising; that which is without arising is the initial aspiration for enlightenment (prathamacittotpāda). By means of this, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattikadharmakṣānti).
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment makes their intention firm, they should generate this bodhicitta as being like a diamond (vajra).
“What is meant by generating the resolve that is like a vajra?
There are ten practices for the generation of the bodhisattva’s resolve that make it like a vajra. What are these ten?”
First, to wander through the perils of immeasurable births and deaths;
second, to give away all that one possesses without any stinginess;
third, to always maintain an impartial mind toward all sentient beings.
The fourth is: "I shall deliver all sentient beings, delivering them by means of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
The fifth is: "Having delivered sentient beings, there is no one at all who has reached parinirvāṇa, because one understands that all dharmas are unarisen.
The sixth is: "To discern and clearly understand all dharmas."
Seventh, they constantly apply diligent effort without omission;
eighth, their wisdom enters everywhere, reaching all things without exception;
ninth, they possess all-knowledge and penetrate through the single gateway.
The tenth is: regarding all that is cherished and held dear, there is neither increase nor decrease; one does not sever attachments through greedy attachment.
These are the ten matters of a bodhisattva’s resolve whose mind is like a diamond; this is the essential compendium of the Buddhas.
The Buddha said:
“Furthermore, there is the arousal of the bodhicitta by which a bodhisattva gives rise to no manifold perceptions within the triple world, nor does he give rise to the perception of non-perception.
Moreover, the Essential Collection of the Buddhas states that one should practice the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).”

What are these six? There is the mundane *dānapāramitā*, which is submerged in the secular world and does not transcend it; there is also the transcendent *dānapāramitā*, which does not fall into the secular.

The same applies to the *śīla*, *kṣānti*, *vīrya*, *dhyāna*, and *prajñāpāramitā*: there may be the practice of the mundane *prajñāpāramitā* that does not transcend the world, or there may be the practice of the transcendent *prajñāpāramitā* that does not fall into the secular.
"What is meant by the mundane *dānapāramitā* which does not transcend the world?

In this regard, a bodhisattva practices extensive giving, providing for śramaṇas, heterodox practitioners (*bāhyaka*), brahmins, the poor, beggars, and those who are distressed; he gives food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty; he gives vehicles, elephants, horses, beds, bedding, clothing, gold, silver, and precious jewels; and even his wife, children, sons, daughters, kingdoms, cities, towns, and villages. He gives away all external possessions of whatever kind without any sense of attachment or regret. Having performed such giving, he calculates in terms of a self and relies upon that which he has given."

Now I have brought forth this gift and that person has accepted it; as a donor, I have no greed or regret. Following the Buddha’s teaching, I practice the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*); now, with a mind of reciprocal giving, I dedicate the merit to all classes of sentient beings, and through this encouragement and assistance, may my act of giving cause all sentient beings to forever attain peace and security.
One who performs such giving has three attachments and hindrances.
What are these three?
First, calculating "self" and "mine."
Second, calculating others;
third, calculating a gift given out of deluded thought;
these constitute the mundane dānapāramitā, which does not transcend the world.
Why is this so? Because they remain entangled in worldly existence and cannot attain liberation.
What is meant by the perfection of giving that transcends the world and does not fall back into the mundane?
It can purify three categories. What are these three?
First, when this bodhisattva practices giving, they do not apprehend a self.
Second, not perceiving a recipient while taking anything;
third, never entertaining deluded thoughts when giving that seek a reward in return—
these are called the three.

There are bodhisattvas who practice giving to encourage and assist all sentient beings; if they give to sentient beings without perceiving a recipient or anything that is taken, they thereby encourage and assist them toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
When one does not scrutinize or perceive the dharma of the food taken, this is called the supramundane *dānapāramitā*. Why is this so?
Because it attains the supramundane.
"What is meant by 'being in the mundane world'?
It refers to being covered by the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).
To be able to relinquish these five is called 'crossing over the world'."
To be without self and without conceptualization, to have nothing upon which to rely and to be entirely without attachment—this is called transcending the world (*lokottara*).

If, having already received the precepts, one thinks that others violate the prohibitions and do not act according to the Dharma; or if one instructs various disciples, thinking, "Because of me they have attained deliverance, and I shall become a Buddha to rescue and aid all beings," yet still reckons oneself as having a body and fails to understand its fundamental non-existence—this is merely the mundane *pāramitā*, and does not lead to transcending the world.

Although they uphold the precepts, they do not conceive of a self; they do not perceive others as violating the Dharma or disrupting the prohibitions, but deliver them all with equanimity. They do not abandon birth and death, yet they do not rely on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Although they liberate sentient beings, they fully realize that they are fundamentally without origin. Patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom are likewise thus.
Those who are without attachment should transcend the world; those who have attachment fall into the mundane.

Furthermore, regarding the secular writings, commentaries, incantations, verses, calculations, the Five Classics and Six Arts, the archives of kings, and the practices of immortals—if one possesses the wisdom of what is studied while harboring expectations, this is the prajñāpāramitā that falls into the mundane.

If one does not regard any worldly aspirations as wisdom, but understands the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; if one views the three periods of time as equal, being without past, future, or present; if one regards the three evil realms as equal and realizes the oneness of the Dharmakāya; if one neither abides in saṃsāra nor dwells in nirvāṇa; and if one transforms and enlightens all beings while universally abiding nowhere—this is the world-transcending Prajñāpāramitā, the essential compendium of the Buddhas.
When these words were spoken, seven hundred *nayutas* of bodhisattvas in the Buddha-land of Devendra attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The trichiliocosm shook in six ways, the heavens rained down various flowers, and a great radiance shone universally throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Essential Compendium* refers to the locus entered by the Bodhisattva stage. What is meant by "stage," and what is meant by "entering"?

Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is nothing whatsoever to enter; all phenomena neither come nor go, and no phenomenon whatsoever is lost. One does not contemplate the stages of the path, nor is there any conceptualization; one cultivates those stages without perceiving any location.
What is meant by "cultivating and purifying that ground"?
For a bodhisattva training in the first dwelling, there are ten dharmas. What are these ten?
First, to have a nature that is pure and harmonious;
second, to feel compassion for all sentient beings;
third, to possess an impartial mind desiring to rescue all living beings.
Fourth, to delight in practicing charity and providing relief to those in poverty;
fifth, to draw near to virtuous friends to inquire about and resolve one's deficiencies;
sixth, to study and seek out the sūtras to enlighten and transform one's doubts.
Seventh, to frequently contemplate renouncing the household life and not longing for worldly occupations;
eighth, to resolve to seek the Buddha-body and realize its formlessness;
ninth, to expound the gift of Dharma to demonstrate it to those who have not yet attained it.
Tenth: to eliminate self-conceit and always maintain sincerity and faith.
These are the ten dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment].
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the second stage, they should always diligently practice eight dharmas.
What are the eight?
First, to uphold the precepts with purity and without defilement;
second, to constantly cultivate filial piety and mindfulness of repaying kindness and virtue.
Third, to abide in the power of patience, taking forbearance as the foundation;
fourth, to practice with reverence and diligence, always maintaining a joyful mind;
fifth, not to abandon any class of sentient beings.
Sixth, practicing the perfection of compassion without ever forgetting or abandoning it;
seventh, revering teachers and elders as if they were the World-Honored One;
eighth, applying oneself with diligence to seek all the perfections (pāramitās).
These are the eight.
"When a bodhisattva practices the third stage, there are five dharmas. What are these five?
First, to seek extensive learning without ever becoming weary or satisfied;
second, to expound and manifest the Dharma that is free from the concerns of food and clothing;
third, to apply the roots of virtue one has cultivated toward the adornment of Buddha-fields.
The fourth is to feel weary of and loathsome toward the hardships of immeasurable birth and death;
the fifth is to abide in a sense of shame and always maintain a feeling of remorse.
These are the five.
"When a Bodhisattva practices the four stages of abiding, there are further ten dharmas. What are these ten?
First is: dwelling in seclusion and constantly maintaining a mind of tranquility."
Second, knowing the proper limits and keeping the mind fixed on contentment;
third, abandoning frivolous play and mocking chatter;
fourth, always being cautious regarding the prohibitions and precepts, never violating them.
Fifth, to feel weary of the five desires and to abide in a state of harmony;
sixth, to resolve the mind so as to attain ultimate accomplishment;
seventh, to be able to bestow all that one possesses in charity, with a mind free from attachment.
Eighth, his mind is always courageous and free from timidity;
ninth, he cherishes nothing among all that he possesses;
tenth, he bestows upon sentient beings the roots of virtue he has accumulated.
These are the ten.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva trains in the five abodes, there are another ten dharmas. What are these ten?
First, to renounce domestic affairs;
second, to distance oneself from bhikṣuṇīs;
third, to cast away thoughts of stinginess and envy regarding one's lineage.
The fourth is to distance oneself from the factions of noisy and tumultuous assemblies;
the fifth is to relinquish the roots of anger, strife, and litigation;
the sixth is not to praise one's own person nor to disparage others.
Seventh, to eliminate the ten evil deeds and the mind of arrogance;
eighth, to constantly reap away the four inversions and teachings that do not accord with the truth;
ninth, to prune away greed, lust, anger, and delusion.
The tenth is: to eliminate attachment to obstructive and deluded thoughts. These are the ten.
"A Bodhisattva who trains in the sixth stage should fully possess the six dharmas and the perfections (pāramitās), and should not practice the six matters."
What are the six? First, his mind is serene and seeks not the state of a śrāvaka;
second, his mind is clear and enlightened and does not long for the state of a pratyekabuddha.
Third, his mind does not abandon any sentient being;
fourth, upon seeing those who beg, he harbors no timidity or weakness;
fifth, he has never practiced the dharma of sorrow or dejection.
The sixth is: not to long for high or elaborately adorned seats.
This is the sixth.
"When a bodhisattva trains in the seventh stage, they relinquish twenty matters."
What are the twenty? First, not reckoning the body;
second, not reckoning the person;
3. Not reckoning a lifespan; 4. Not reckoning life;
5. Not reckoning annihilation;
Sixth, not reckoning [things] as permanent;
seventh, not harboring expectations or conceptualizations;
eighth, not maintaining views regarding retribution and response.
9. Not perceiving name-and-form;
10. Not relying upon the five aggregates;
11. Not craving the four great elements.
12. Not relying on the entrance of decline;
13. Not being attached to the three realms;
14. Not associating with evil.
Fifteenth, eternal peace and non-attachment;
sixteenth, performing no action within the realm of non-existence;
seventeenth, not even clinging to the Buddha, up to and including the ultimate.
Eighteenth, never having followed the sixty-two views;
nineteenth, fully understanding all dharmas and not slandering emptiness;
twentieth, fully knowing that there is no fundamental basis and thus harboring no aspiration for the Path.
By practicing this Dharma, one is endowed with twenty matters.
What are these twenty? They are:

understanding the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), clarity regarding the signless (*animitta*), discerning the wishless (*apraṇihita*), purifying the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*), constantly harboring compassion (*karuṇā*), loving all sentient beings, not reckoning sentient beings as real, viewing all phenomena with equanimity, clear comprehension of the gate of cessation (*śamatha*), the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), the unarisen noble wisdom (*ārya-prajñā*), proclaiming the meaning of the single flavor (*ekarasa*), eliminating manifold thoughts, removing all false imaginings (*vikalpa*), abandoning all wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), extinguishing the defilements of dust and toil, calmly contemplating the stages (*bhūmi*), having a mind that is harmonious and pliant, being free from the intent to harm, and being unstained by fetters and attachments. These are the twenty.
"The eighth bodhisattva should practice four dharmas. What are these four?
First, entering among sentient beings with a mind of supernatural wisdom to transform and guide them."
Second, causing those who behold the emptiness of the Buddha-lands to attain the ultimate;
third, prostrating before the Buddha’s body to inquire and receive teachings beyond one's reach;
fourth, having seen the Buddha’s body, observing it with thorough discernment—these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas:
first, to be fully proficient in understanding the fundamental nature of sentient beings and to manifest teachings for them according to their inclinations;
second, to adorn and purify Buddha-fields by diligently and earnestly studying the illusion-like samādhi.
Third, one should deliver those sentient beings who are ready for liberation according to their inclinations;
fourth, one observes the five destinies in which sentient beings are born and liberates them accordingly.
These are the four.

"The ninth bodhisattva should study the foundation of virtuous vows with discernment; whatever they vow, it shall immediately be accomplished. They distinguish the speech and words of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, and then, through their eloquence, preach the Dharma in accordance with those sounds."

From the time within the womb, he fully understood and comprehended everything; likewise, upon being born and falling to the ground, regarding his lineage, his kin, his life as a householder, and his renunciation, as well as sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, adorning the site of enlightenment, and the fulfillment of all meritorious virtues and the Buddha-dharma—there was nothing he did not thoroughly know.

"The tenth bodhisattva should be named Tathāgata-Arhat-Samyaksambuddha; if he enters this dwelling place, that ground is called the Path-ground of all Buddhas, and is titled 'The Essential Collection of the Buddhas'."
"Furthermore, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* is equal to that which is expressed by words, and it enters the gate of emptiness as expressed by words.
What is meant by the 'gate of emptiness as expressed by words'? "
All phenomena are entirely gates of emptiness.
Why are they called empty?
Because they cause future phenomena to be without arising; because they serve as gates for all phenomena to eliminate attachments.
As for the gate of deliverance, it proclaims and clarifies the ultimate beginning and end of all phenomena.
As for the gate of practice, all phenomena are neither discarded nor relinquished, neither submerged nor produced.
As for its "Gate of Names," all dharmas have already transcended names and words; those names are fundamentally pure, neither attained nor lost.

As for its "Gate of Lightness," it completely transcends the delusions of contempt for all dharmas, as well as the origins from which the roots of affection and the causes and conditions of retribution arise.
The Gate of Accordance proclaims and clarifies all dharmas to bring about harmony, stability, and subjugation.
The Gate of Binding releases all dharmas to give rise to profound stillness.
The Gate of Incineration burns away all dharmas to achieve utter purity.
As for the Gate of Radiance, it is without obstruction, attachment, or liberation regarding all phenomena.
As for the Gate of Tendency, it severs the sounds to which all phenomena return, yet does not abandon their fundamental source.
As for the gate of suchness, it is to understand clearly that the primordial source neither advances nor moves.
As for the gate of following, it is to initiate [practice] from all phenomena.
As for the gate of abiding, it is to have no place of abiding within any phenomenon and to harbor no grief or sorrow.
As for those who create the gate, they do not perceive the lineage produced by any phenomena.
As for those who equalize the gate, they cultivate equanimity toward all phenomena and do not regress.
As for the gate of defilement (*mala-mukha*), it consists of reckoning all phenomena as being free from impurity, such that they are without flaw from beginning to end.

As for the gate of reception (*upādāna-mukha*), it consists of grasping all phenomena while realizing they are unattainable; with the mind directed toward the profound and subtle, one attains eternal tranquility regarding the six sense-bases and all phenomena.
As for the gate of the shore, it causes all dharmas to cross over to the other shore, yet it perceives neither this shore nor that shore, nor crossing nor not crossing.
As for the gate of arising, one does not perceive the birth, aging, sickness, or death of any dharma.
As for the gate of contemplation, all dharmas are entirely quiescent; they are neither conceptualized nor abandoned, neither attached to nor detached from.
As for the gate of the Dharma, because the dharma-realm is eternally abiding, it manifests various sutras according to the occasion.
As for its gate of tranquility, all dharmas abide in a state of profound stillness and silence, free from affliction and distress.
As for its gate of emptiness, all dharmas are like space—without beginning or end, and without abiding.
As for the gate of exhaustion, all phenomena are entirely exhausted and do not regress; they are likewise forever extinguished.
As for the gate of abiding, all phenomena are unmoving and nothing can shake them.

As for this gate of wisdom, because one follows that wisdom without practicing any conditioned activities, there is nothing that can be known, yet nothing that is not known; there is no thought and no vision.
This gate is such that among all dharmas there is neither correspondence nor non-correspondence, and neither conjunction nor dispersion, so as to leave its verbal expressions vast and open.
As for the "Opening Gate," although one wanders among all phenomena, one eliminates all doors [of attachment].
As for the "Covering Gate," regarding all phenomena, one removes all coverings, causing one to know emptiness and non-existence, and to abandon the six matters.
As for the gate of mindfulness, it consists of digesting what arises among all phenomena through neither recollecting nor forgetting.
As for the gate of transcendence, it is that all phenomena arise from emptiness as their cause, thereby giving rise to fear and the manifold sufferings born of conditions.
As for "departing from the gate," it means abandoning and severing all calculations of annihilation or permanence regarding all phenomena.
As for "counting the gate," it means that with respect to all phenomena, one does not elevate what has arisen; among all numerical reckonings, there is neither high nor low.
As for those who establish a gate, all phenomena abide; they abide in non-abiding, removing all places of dwelling.

As for those who have no gate, although they exist amidst all phenomena, there is neither coming nor going; they do not stand, do not sit, do not wander, and do not sleep; there is neither that which corresponds nor that which does not correspond.

Regarding the gateway of the aggregates (*skandha*): it abides in all phenomena as being fully complete, without those who cross over or those not crossed over, and without any pervasive limit, like empty space.
Regarding the gateway of the bases (*āyatana*): it consists of understanding and knowing that the arising of the five aggregates within all phenomena is actually without arising.
As for the gate of resonance, it is the understanding that all phenomena are without sound; that is to say, they are resonanceless and eternally free from words and phrases.
As for the gate of differentiation, it is the realization that although one may dwell amidst negligence regarding all phenomena, there is no wandering or racing.
As for the gate of solidity, it clearly understands that all phenomena are disintegrated and that their rigidity is forever extinguished in parinirvāṇa.
As for the gate of dissolution, it fully realizes all phenomena and comprehends their limits; they have no location and no beginning or end, nor do they have birth, just like the World-Honored One.

"Regarding the reckoning of written characters, there is nothing capable of bearing them; even if one were to multiply words and phrases, they would likewise be non-existent. Furthermore, there are no names or characters; there is no speech and no talk. One does not cling to any direction, and there is neither writing nor reading."
The reason for this is that all things are empty and lack substantial reality.
All dharmas are thus: they exist by virtue of this [emptiness], and this is the entry into *dhāraṇī*.
To reckon with non-existence is to proclaim the thorough entry into emptiness; one who can enter this draws near to the practice of a Bodhisattva.

Regarding all written characters, they understand them to be without flaw or affliction; they are not bound or attached by words, yet they discern the sequence from which all phenomena arise and attain the noble wisdom regarding the source of sounds.

"If a bodhisattva enters this gateway of the seal of the emptiness of letters, and whether hearing it or receiving it, maintains it in mind and cherishes it, explaining it to others with a mind that does not falter, they will be able to eliminate twenty kinds of fetters:
first, their resolve shall be firm and not timid;
second, their mindfulness shall always be present and not beclouded."
Third, he is able to walk alone without hesitation or difficulty;
fourth, his mind is firm and strong, harboring no weakness or inferiority;
fifth, his resolve is fixed on shame and remorse regarding what he has not yet attained.
Sixth, his mind is capable of awakening to and comprehending all things without fail;
seventh, his wisdom is so lofty that there is none it does not illuminate;
eighth, his eloquence is such that there is not a single point of obstruction.
Ninth, they attain dhāraṇī, whereby all that they have heard is fully retained without ever being forgotten;
tenth, they eliminate the web of doubt and are free from hesitation;
eleventh, they achieve thorough penetration and harbor no lingering uncertainty.
Twelfth, wherever they dwell or reside among people, they harbor no feelings of increase or decrease;
thirteenth, their speech is gentle and harmonious, and there are none who do not bow their heads in reverence;
fourteenth, even if they hear harsh words, they do not become distressed or sorrowful.
Fifteenth, his nature is not impetuous, but is always serene;
sixteenth, he clearly understands and discriminates sounds and resonances in whatever place he dwells;

seventeenth, he thoroughly comprehends the five aggregates (*skandha*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the various sense bases (*āyatana*) as well as their retributive causes and conditions.
Eighteenth, he analyzes and distinguishes all dharmas, attaining thorough penetration and clear understanding of them; knowing the thoughts in people's minds, he preaches the Dharma for them.

Nineteenth, he knows what is possible and what is impossible, as well as limits and the limitless; he understands wisdom and clearly masters skillful means (*upāya*), transforming beings according to the times.

Twentieth, he discerns the matters of advancing and retreating, entering and exiting, as well as dignified conduct and ritual propriety; understanding shame and modesty, he wields the firm sword to enter wherever he may go, giving rise to the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.
"Regarding this teaching on the gateway of the empty seal of letters: if one hears it, receives it, upholds it, recites it, or even merely hears it, ten meritorious benefits shall be attained:
first, in every lifetime one will not receive a female body;
second, one will abandon all hardships and the eight unfavorable conditions."
Third, wherever they dwell or reside, they always obtain leisure and do not harbor any sense of haste;
fourth, they constantly encounter the era of a Buddha and, upon seeing the World-Honored One, immediately give rise to joy and gladness;
fifth, their minds are expansive and steady as they make offerings to the Great Sage.
Sixth, the Tathāgata perceives their minds and preaches the sūtras for them;
seventh, upon hearing what is preached, they immediately practice it accordingly;
eighth, they soon attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Ninth, through clearly understanding the wisdom of emptiness, one attains the state of non-arising;
tenth, one swiftly accomplishes the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
This is the Essential Collection of the Buddha.

"Furthermore, that which is proclaimed as the Essential Collection of the Buddha is equal to the three periods of time; it purifies the three spheres, attains the state of non-arising, and gives birth to the Dharma of True Reality. It brings understanding of the triple world and thoroughly dispels lust, anger, and delusion. It is naturally without pleasure, without annihilation, without permanence, without location, and without abiding."
The three vehicles converge upon a single gate; they penetrate all dharmas without contention, entering that which is peerless, without movement or progression, and beyond thought or comparison.
"Furthermore, as for reckoning the Buddha: he has never awakened to or attained supreme perfect enlightenment; he does not resolve all phenomena, nor does he know or acquire them.

The Buddha does not attain wisdom, yet he is not without wisdom; he is not joined with worldly afflictions, yet he is without resentment and does not realize a final cessation; he neither attains nor is obstructed, yet he has no active engagement, and he does not abide even in equanimity."

The Buddha neither attains the Way nor loses anything; there is no Dharma and no assembly. The Buddha does not attain Buddhahood, nor does he conceive of bodhisattvas. He is neither liberated nor bound; all sentient beings are fundamentally and utterly pure.
The Buddha does not see dharmas, does not hear them, and does not think of them; nor does he have anything to teach. The Honored One has nothing to say and no words.

"Those who understand all Buddhas know that there are no words and that from the beginning no sounds were uttered; in future ages, likewise, nothing shall be proclaimed. He does not instruct others to speak, for there is neither wisdom nor lack of wisdom."

The Buddha is not the one who bestows blessings, nor is he the merit that constitutes the completion of blessings for all beings. The Buddha does not eat or drink, nor does he bestow food upon others.
The Buddha has no body and no physical form; do not perceive the Tathāgata as having a material body, for he is without marks and without signs of beauty.
There are no sūtras nor a dharma-realm; the Buddha neither appears nor does he eternally abide; he has never entered parinirvāṇa, nor is there anything that enters extinction. Why is this so?

Because all dharmas are eternally extinguished, the Buddha does not stand alone nor dwell among a great assembly; there is no one who can see the Buddha, nor anyone who hears him, and there is no making of offerings.
In reckoning the various Buddha-dharmas, there are neither many nor are they one.
The Buddha does not attain a path, nor does he seek a location; he neither turns the wheel of Dharma nor does he retreat.

The Buddha is like a provisional designation; that which is reckoned as the Buddha, his voice is likewise like [that designation]. The sounds of the past and the future are no different; the past and the future are equal. That which is equal has no partiality;

that which has no partiality has no limitlessness; that which has no limitlessness has no end or death; that which has no end or death does not employ medicine—this is the essential compendium of the Buddha.

"The reason for proclaiming what the Buddha has taught is out of a desire to compassionately deliver sentient beings; the Buddha has no essential compendium, nor does he make distinctions, nor does he discourse upon the meaning of an essential compendium."

When the Tathāgata Heavenly King expounded upon the meaning of this Sūtra, the Compendium of the Essentials of All Buddhas, twelve thousand bodhisattvas in the world of Universal Radiance all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the bodhisattvas did not see any of the several hundred million buddhas at all, but beheld only the single Buddha, the Tathāgata Deva-rāja.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, remaining in the Sahā world, thought to himself:

"Today, the World-Honored Buddhas of the ten directions, each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have all come together at the place of the Buddha Deva-rāja in the eastern buddha-field, to collectively proclaim the essential Dharma of the *Buddhasaṃgītisūtra*."
"I should now go to that world to pay homage to the Buddhas and receive the sūtras from them.

Although I have constantly traveled throughout the ten directions, prostrating before the Buddhas and listening to the Dharma they preach, it is only now that they have all gathered together in a single buddha-field. Such a rare and unprecedented opportunity is difficult to encounter; such a supreme, holy land appearing in the world cannot be met again, and is difficult to see or hear."
Mañjuśrī replied to Maitreya:

"Let us go together to the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Devarāja, the Land of Universal Radiance. There, countless hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas have all assembled; let us together proclaim the essential Dharma-collection of the Buddhas, and listen to it while beholding those Buddhas."
"Why is this? Because all the Great Holy Ones have assembled in one place, and such an encounter is difficult to meet.
Maitreya Bodhisattva replied to Mañjuśrī:
"Virtuous one, if you wish to go, you may proceed on your way; I shall not go. Why is this?

The assembly of the Buddhas possesses a majesty of virtue and wisdom so sublime that it is beyond comparison; my body cannot see it, nor am I capable of beholding their forms or hearing their voices."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Do not perceive the Tathāgatas by means of their physical forms; for the Buddha is the Dharma-body, and the Dharma-body is invisible, inaudible, and cannot be nourished.
Mañjuśrī asked, "Do you not make offerings to the Tathāgata? Maitreya replied:
"I do not make offerings. Why is this?
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is beyond being offered to; since there is fundamentally no Tathāgata, there is no duality."
Mañjuśrī spoke again: "What is meant by 'non-duality'? Maitreya replied:
"That which is non-dual means being without attachment, being beyond measure, and being without variety.
What is called 'non-dual' does not create dualistic karma."
What are called the two karmas?

To say that these afflictions involve harboring resentment and giving rise to such views of arising and ceasing as: "This is upholding the precepts" and "This is violating the prohibitions," thus falsely conceptualizing this and that—this is called duality. To say:
"This is a śrāvaka" and "This is a pratyekabuddha," [and] "This is a samyaksaṃbuddha."
To conceptualize in this way is to create duality.
To conceive of oneself as a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or a buddha—holding such notions—is what is called duality.
To abandon this dharma and to practice and realize that dharma—these are two.
To differentiate wisdom and the wisdom that does not understand. Suppose, Mañjuśrī!
Holding fast to mindfulness and the two types of wisdom, with the resolve to advance or retreat, one ascends to the contemplation of the Buddha and thereby creates two karmas.
Throughout a kalpa or even beyond a kalpa, I shall expound upon these various dualities; the eloquence I manifest will be inexhaustible.
Why is this? Because when one calculates all dualities, there are no two; whatever can be proclaimed enters entirely into the single meaning, for all dharmas are without plurality.
Mañjuśrī replied:

"Your body has now fallen into a great perversion; all dharmas are entirely unarisen, yet you insist on making distinctions and, with various kinds of words, conversely lament your own self. Even if I were to spend an eon or more than an eon, my eloquence would never be exhausted."
Maitreya replied, "Because words based on letters involve attachment, one should examine all phenomena as being truly without the characteristic of arising and as being immovable.
Then, Mañjuśrī addressed the other bodhisattvas:
“Sons of good family!
Let us all go together to the abode of the Buddha Tathāgata Devendra, to behold the Tathāgatas and listen to what they preach.
Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa replied to Mañjuśrī:
“The Tathāgata, the Arhat, is impossible to behold; for what reason, O Venerable One, do you utter this teaching that we should go together to see the Tathāgata?
Where is the Tathāgata, whom you wish to see?”

I have heard the Buddha say that the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, neither comes nor goes; since I now reckon that all dharmas of the three periods of time are entirely empty and non-existent, he cannot be seen.
Yet just now, Mañjuśrī spoke these words, saying that he had gone to see the Tathāgata.
With what kind of eye does one behold the Tathāgata?
Is it with the fleshly eye that one sees him,
or is it by means of the divine eye?
If one uses the fleshly eye, the fleshly eye sees nothing. Why is this?
Because the fleshly eye is empty; being empty, there is nothing to be seen.
"If one uses the divine eye, yet reckons that within the divine eye there is no conceptualization, then one cannot see the Tathāgata through conceptualization.
Mañjuśrī replied: "According to what you, son of good family, are currently contemplating, there is neither a Tathāgata nor any sūtra; there is neither seeing nor nourishing."
As the intention of Prajñākūṭa’s inquiry suggests, one may indeed speak of and differentiate verbal expressions.

Yet, the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and the coming and going of sentient beings who offer worship and service—all these rely upon words; since words are inherently empty, they are said to be equal. This is what is meant.
The Tathāgata is without speech, without origin, and without transition; all things are naturally empty, and these two matters are entirely equal.
The Tathāgata is without speech, without origin, and without transition. Those who are capable may advance together with him; as for those who are unwilling, I shall go alone.
"Formless yet manifesting form, he does not dwell in the realm of matter;
desiring to transform and enlighten the multitudes, he manifests a body to provide instruction.
The Buddha is a gathering beyond form, nor does he cling to conditioned phenomena."
"Having transcended all numerical limits, the Teacher has thus manifested his body.
