Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty:
At that time, Mañjuśrī was insatiable in his thirst for the Dharma and free from weariness;
yet, being alone without a companion and constrained by the Buddha’s spiritual power, not a single person from that assembly followed him.

Mañjuśrī, in the brief interval of time it takes to extend one's arm, suddenly vanished from the Sahā world and arrived at the realm of Universal Radiance, where he was in the presence of the Buddha Heavenly King.
At that time, Mañjuśrī circumambulated the trichiliocosm seven times, prostrated before all the Buddhas, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that moment, on the right side of the Tathāgata King of Devas, there was a woman named Vigatārtha, who sat cross-legged, absorbed in the samādhi of Universal Moon Stainless Radiance.
At that time, the Buddha Tathāgata Devendra thought to himself:

"Mañjuśrī is praised by all Buddhas; he practices the profound and subtle patience of emptiness-wisdom, such that none can equal him, and he takes void stillness and silence as his meritorious achievement."

Now, having arisen from the realm of endurance with thoughts in mind, you have fallen into great perversion; clinging intensely to a self, you have a destination toward which you are heading—you shall be driven back and established upon the summit of Mount Cakravāḍa.

For this reason, you shall expound the Dharma that is infinitely profound and subtle, and you shall manifest a great radiance for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattvas in the future. Why is this so?
The Dharma of all Buddhas is inconceivable; it is majestic and immeasurable, profound and unattainable.

Mañjuśrī is foremost in extensive learning, and his wisdom of the Way is transcendent and extraordinary; even as vast as the emptiness of the ten directions, he can cause [beings] to abide upon the summit of Mount Cakravāḍa, and only then is he able to inspire all sentient beings.
The Tathāgata Devendra addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Having come here, what do you wish to observe? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
While I was in this Sahā world, I thought to myself:

'The appearance of Buddhas in the world is extremely rare to encounter; the preaching of the sūtras is likewise difficult to meet. Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years, the Buddhas of the ten directions have all come together in the Samantaprabhāsa world to proclaim the essential Dharma of the *Saṃnipāta*. "
"I shall go to visit and behold all the Tathāgatas to hear the Dharma they preach; for the sake of the Dharma, I have come to this buddha-field.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata Heavenly King, just as he had intended, entered into samādhi and manifested his supernormal powers, transporting Mañjuśrī so that he stood naturally upon the summit of Mount Cakravāḍa.
Unaware of who had lifted him up to this mountain peak, he thought to himself:
"What strange marvel is this?

While I was amidst the great assembly, possessing lofty and immeasurable majesty and peerless excellence, dwelling within the pure and solemn *bodhimaṇḍa* of the Great Sages, I have suddenly arrived here atop the Cakravāḍa mountains. Who has done this?"
He immediately understood that this was a miraculous manifestation produced by the Tathāgata Devendra.
Mañjuśrī then thought to himself:
"What auspicious omen is there that such a transformation has occurred?"
While remaining naturally present within this great assembly, the woman Vimālaprabhā sat to the right of the Tathāgata Devendrarāja; she was not moved, but I alone was shifted.

Furthermore, that woman possesses roots of virtue that are pure and peerless; she has deeply entered the patience of the Dharma and attained an inexhaustible dhāraṇī—does she not surpass me? Why is this so?
"Instead of sending her away, you have instead brought me here.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"Now, manifesting the power of spiritual transformations through the majesty of his divine feet, and displaying the force of the Way through boundless noble wisdom, he has returned to the assembly."
Thereupon, in accordance with that form, he entered into meditative absorption and manifested supernormal powers.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, he leaped across Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges to the east, yet he could not leave them far behind.
"That Buddha-world is as large as a single hair; how much more so, then, could one enter the assemblies of those Buddhas?

At that time, Mañjuśrī again traveled to immeasurable worlds in the ten directions and manifested transformations through his majestic power and spiritual strength, yet he was still unable to re-enter the assemblies of those Buddhas.
Why is this so? It is because they are established by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas.

Mañjuśrī traveled throughout the countless billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of lands in the ten directions, and then immediately returned to stay atop the Cakravāḍa Mountains, where he reflected to himself:

“The noble intent established by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possesses immeasurable majestic power and a sublime, far-reaching path-wisdom that cannot be grasped or compared; it is beyond the reach of my own supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*), and one cannot compete with them in the exercise of such powers.”

Why is this so? The Dharma taught by all Buddhas is never false or vain; they walk alone throughout the ten directions without peer. It is simply that my own body is insufficient, such that I am unable to hear and receive their teaching of the Dharma.

The Dharma of all Tathāgatas has never been mutually contradictory; all Buddhas regard sentient beings with an impartial mind. It would be better to practice the four foundations of mindfulness and enter meditative absorption here upon the summit of this Mount Cakravāḍa.
Mañjuśrī further thought to himself: "What is meant by 'application of mindfulness' (smṛtyupasthāna)?
It means that there is no mind, yet one does not fail to contemplate all phenomena; all phenomena have no location, nor do they abide anywhere."
By what means is there non-abiding?
Because there is no location.
Who is it that thoroughly elucidates the beginning and end to dispel all phenomena?
The place where one dwells is itself without dwelling; this is what constitutes a dwelling place.
These four foundations of mindfulness dwell in non-dwelling, which means there is no intention and no mental recollection.

While Mañjuśrī was thus practicing these four foundations of mindfulness, forty-two thousand sons of gods went to his location, prostrated at his feet, rained down celestial flowers and incense as an offering to Mañjuśrī, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, there was a son of heaven named Prabhāketu who asked Mañjuśrī,
“By what concentration and by what practice of the path did you just now arise? Mañjuśrī replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
You now turn back and ask me:
‘By means of what samādhi do you now arise after having practiced and cultivated it?’”

"As for this practiced concentration, it is a state that even the Great Sages, the Buddhas, cannot attain, and the same is true for the Śrāvakas. By means of this concentrated mind, one follows and practices; through this practice, one causes all sentient beings—possessing lust, anger, and delusion alike—to follow this path which I uphold."
Then the Devaputra Prabhāketu asked:
"What kind of practice is this,
that which even the Great Sages, the Buddhas, cannot attain?"
He replied: "It is the practice of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—the sphere that even the Great Sages, the Buddhas, cannot attain.
The devaputra asked again:
“The place that the Great Sages, the Buddhas, cannot attain— is it there that you, O Benevolent One, now practice this conduct? Mañjuśrī replied,
“If there were such a practice, I would indeed practice it.”
That which was practiced previously is, in truth, never practiced at all. Why is this so?
Because all dharmas are entirely quiescent.
He asked the devaputra:
"By means of what concentration do you practice and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness?
The devaputra replied:
"What is meant by 'the foundations of mindfulness,' such that all dharmas are without intention and without thought?
The devaputra asked again:
"If there is neither intention nor thought, how can there be any practice?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "To be without intention and without thought is the foremost practice; this alone is the practice of equality. When one's practice is equal, there is no partiality;

when there is no partiality, there are no five destinies. When there are no five destinies, one does not perceive the root of delusion; when there is no root of delusion, the light of wisdom is not produced. That which does not produce light has nothing that arises; that which has nothing that arises has nothing that perishes. That which has nothing that perishes has no discipline; that which has no discipline has nothing that is accomplished. That which has nothing that is accomplished has nothing that is destroyed. This absence of destruction is called 'purity from beginning to end'; it is the practice of the noble ones, forever free from worldly defilement."
He asked Mañjuśrī again,
"What is meant by 'defilements'? Mañjuśrī replied:
When that consciousness regresses and takes pleasure in the Buddha-wisdom, this is called *kleśa* (affliction).

To undergo conceptualization and calculate the existence of a body; to have things upon which one relies and from which one gives rise to discursive thought; to be arrogant and self-important; to have objects of longing, hope, and vows; to calculate, weigh, and measure distances near and far; and to contemplate and observe whether thoughts are appropriate or inappropriate—[these constitute affliction].

Having eliminated arrogance yet calculating toward annihilation, the mind conceives of permanence; dwelling within that which is non-apprehended, one returns to what is seen, grasping at existence while experiencing non-existence, even to the point of indulging in heedless thoughts and frivolity. To attempt to weigh such a mind in order to reach equanimity—calculating such practices as being the law of the noble ones—is entirely nothing but worldly defilement.
Then the devaputra Prabhāketu praised him, saying: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī!”
"Speak these words quickly, so that you may practice these four foundations of mindfulness.
Mañjuśrī then addressed him, saying: "Do not engage in false conceptualization.

Within all names and forms, there is nothing produced and nothing accomplished; furthermore, there is neither the present nor any verbal expression. It is only for the sake of convenience that one speaks according to the occasion. All dharmas neither abide nor do they not abide; yet you conversely praise me, saying 'Excellent!'"
He asked the devaputra again:
"If one does not speak of the foundations of mindfulness, they cannot be explained; nor is there anyone able to lecture on their intended meaning through words. Why is this so?"

All dharmas are entirely beyond verbal expression; wishing to proclaim all dharmas, one finds them to be indivisible, for there has never been a fixed teaching, yet each is guided and transformed according to the appropriate time.
Then, Prabhāketu asked Mañjuśrī:
"What you have just said conforms to all foolish ordinary beings; it accords with their dwelling places and their practice of lust, anger, and delusion, and it arises from abiding in such conduct."
"In what do foolish worldlings abide when they practice lust, anger, and delusion?

Mañjuśrī replied, "Foolish worldlings abide in non-existence; they practice lust, anger, and delusion while established in the *dharmadhātu*, dwelling at the primordial limit (*koṭi*) while abiding in the absence of a basis."

Why is this so? Your Majesty, you should know that wherever the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) resides, it cannot be differentiated and cannot be described; its fundamental beginning and limit are likewise thus.
The devaputra asked again:
"What is meant by 'the original limit' (pūrvakoṭi) that you speak of? Mañjuśrī replied:
"The original state of sentient beings is called the 'Fundamental Limit' (bhūtakoṭi).
The Devaputra asked again:
"What is meant by the 'original state of sentient beings'?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "The root of birth and death is the source of sentient beings.
The devaputra asked again:
"What is meant by the root of birth and death? Mañjuśrī replied:
"The root of empty space is the source of birth and death, O Devaputra."

The realm of empty space is, from its original limit, uninterrupted and without boundaries; it is neither long nor short, neither coarse nor fine, neither broad nor narrow, neither distant nor near, neither square nor round. That which is called "empty space" is merely a provisional designation and is likewise without name.
All phenomena are likewise thus: they are like empty space, existing only as provisional names.

Just as empty space is neither born nor does it age, neither falls ill nor grows old, and likewise does not die; it has no rebirth, no delusive thoughts, harbors no resentment, suffers no loss, and experiences no non-loss—it is entirely without attachment. It harbors no sorrow or grief. All phenomena take this as their ultimate resort, yet this single limit of reality (ekānta) has no place of return and is beyond calculation.
"Son of Heaven, you should know that all dharmas have neither advancement nor retreat, neither conjunction nor dispersion; they cannot be grasped, for they have no location.
Therefore, Son of Heaven!"

All dharmas are entirely without location, without aspiration, without leading or not leading, and without established rules; this is because all dharmas are entirely equal and without partiality. Therefore, they are said to be "without root," for their very non-existence is thus.
When these words were spoken, the assembly of devaputras all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, the devaputras, abiding in the emptiness of dharmas, practiced with reverence and veneration; they then rained down celestial flowers, scattering them as an offering over Mañjuśrī.
Through the majestic spiritual power (*prabhāva*) of Mañjuśrī, all the flowers remained suspended in mid-air without anyone holding them, as if they had grown from roots.
Mañjuśrī addressed Prabhāketu: "What do you think, O Son of Heaven?"
"Now, upon what do these flowers depend for their abiding?
The devaputra replied,
"They abide nowhere."
Mañjuśrī replied: "Therefore, O Devaputra, you should know that all phenomena abide in non-abiding;
they abide like space, like emptiness—unmoving, neither falling nor wavering, without recollection and without conceptualization."
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are equal to empty space; therefore, they are unmoving, do not fall, and do not waver.
Then, Prabhāketu addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“O Benevolent One!

Your supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) are so majestic as to be beyond measure; in the mere instant of forming a thought, you reach hundreds of thousands of millions of countless lands in the ten directions and return immediately thereafter.”
Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Buddhas do not attain immeasurable supernormal powers, transformations, or majestic spiritual authority, nor can the śrāvakas and others reach such levels. Why is this?
The boundless wisdom of the Path cannot even be heard of, so how could it be attained!

The supernormal powers attained by all ignorant, ordinary worldlings are those which all Buddhas, all bodhisattvas, and all śrāvakas have not obtained throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; they have never attained them, nor shall they ever attain them.
Only all foolish ordinary people can obtain this alone. What do they obtain?

They obtain the notions of self, person, life-span, and vital consciousness; they hold views of annihilationism or eternalism; and they obtain lust, anger, and ignorance—things which the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not obtain.
That which is called "attainment" is not something that the Path brings forth; it is that which is unarisen, yet causes that which is unarisen to arise.
Therefore, O Son of Heaven! That which is attained by all foolish, ordinary worldlings cannot be reached even by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, disciples, or Pratyekabuddhas.
When the Buddhas had finished speaking this Essential Collection of All Buddhas, each returned to their own place.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Heavenly King thought to himself:
"I should manifest my response so that Mañjuśrī shall return to this place!"

Then, the Buddha Tathāgata Devendra relinquished his supernormal power and emitted purple-gold light from his right palm; this radiance shone upon Mañjuśrī, circling him seven times before vanishing into the crown of Mañjuśrī’s head.
Mañjuśrī immediately understood that the Tathāgata Heavenly King desired to see him.
Mañjuśrī then said to Prabhāketu:
"We should go together to the Tathāgata Heavenly King, prostrate ourselves in salutation, and inquire about the profound and subtle meanings he intends to teach as a Dharma-gate."
The devaputra replied, “Excellent!
Go; you should know that now is the time.”

In the mere instant that Mañjuśrī conceived this thought, together with Kāñcanaprabhāketu, he suddenly vanished from the summit of the Cakravāḍa Mountains and appeared before the Tathāgata Devendra. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side with palms joined in reverence;
the sons of the gods from the worlds of the ten directions did likewise.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, the Heavenly King:

"If good men and good women alike plant the roots of virtue and cultivate the profound and wondrous Dharma, they should not harbor doubts; having become vessels of the Dharma, all shall receive its grace."

Why is this? Because I see that the Great Sages surpass even the dragon-elephants, and since these Great Sages have already assembled together, I remain outside and am not included among their number.
Separated from such profound and wondrous Dharma principles, I remain alone with this woman’s body, sitting here steadfastly without moving or shifting, nor do I see her departing.

As I have observed such sighs of lamentation regarding the essential points of these infinitely subtle and wondrous sutras, I have instead been transferred to dwell upon the summit of Mount Cakravāḍa.

I recall that once, during the time it takes to eat a single meal, I traveled throughout the countless Buddha-lands of the eastern direction—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—to prostrate before the Buddhas, listen to the Dharma they expounded, and retain it in my heart; I questioned the Buddhas to resolve my doubts, yet I never once perceived myself being sent away to another Buddha-land.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, having observed my resolve, had previously exhorted me to proclaim the Way of the Sūtras; yet now, the Great Sage has instead transferred me to the summit of Mount Cakravāḍa. It is here that I shall propagate the boundless Dharma teachings, bringing great joy to many who all thirst for and look up to them. Starving for the transformative influence of the Path and its various teachings, my mind is restless with the desire to behold the Tathāgata, and I have uttered these thoughts:
"For what reason am I alone transferred away from this assembly, while the woman Liyi remains there peacefully without coming forth?"
He further reflected:

"The sūtras and teachings expounded by the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, cannot be subverted or distorted. It is not that my mind does not accept them; rather, it is because I am inferior and lack the vessel for the Dharma he teaches, which is why he has moved me here alone, yet did not move this woman."
The Tathāgata Devendra replied to Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Regarding the sūtras and teachings proclaimed by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, you, O Benevolent One, have nothing therein that you should not accept."

Furthermore, the path-wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is profound and extraordinary, beyond reach; for this reason, it cannot be expounded as an ordinary, uniform collection of the essentials of all Buddhas according to one's own will.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
When I previously set out from the Sahā world, I thought to myself:

'Now, in the Samantaprabhā world, the meaning of the sūtra *The Essential Collection of the Buddha's Teachings* is being expounded; I shall go there to pay homage to the Buddhas and listen to the Dharma they proclaim.'"
At that time, he fell into great hardship, dwelling in infinite inversion and improper thoughts.
Having come from that land desiring to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma he preached, he nevertheless remained bound by three obstacles; harboring this intention, he arrived at this buddha-field.
What are these three?
First, attaining one's own body;
second, attaining all Buddhas.
Third, attaining all dharmas.
Mañjuśrī, you should know that one cannot attain the unimpeded wisdom-practice of the bodhisattvas through inverted practice.
What do you think, Mañjuśrī? What is your inclination regarding this?
"Since ancient times, have there been any who were able to behold the Tathāgata?
Can the Tathāgata, in turn, be observed?
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!

When observing phenomena according to ultimate truth, there are neither Buddhas nor dharmas; all dharmas are entirely unarisen, and the Tathāgata is without sight and cannot be perceived as a Buddha.”
"Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely without anything to be seen.
At that time, the Buddha again asked Mañjuśrī:
“By what kind of unobstructed practice of the eye does one wish to see the Tathāgata?
By what kind of clarity of the ear regarding all meanings does one wish to hear the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata?”
Mañjuśrī remained silent and spoke no word.
At that time, the other bodhisattvas in the assembly each thought to themselves:
"Mañjuśrī is truly unable to provide an answer to the Dharma and its meaning as questioned by the Tathāgata."
"Why is this? The Tathāgata has just posed a difficult question, yet remains silent and says nothing.
The Tathāgata Heavenly King, knowing what was in the minds of the bodhisattvas, addressed them:
"Cease, son of good family!
Do not look upon Mañjuśrī with thoughts that he is unattainable. Why is this?

"Having fully perfected the patience regarding the profound Dharma and possessing both skillful means and wisdom, they have attained universal penetration; their wisdom exceeds the void, and they respond to the Tathāgata through silent silence.
The bodhisattvas asked:
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!"
"With what intention did you thoroughly investigate the meaning of wisdom and pose this question?
The World-Honored One replied,
"It is so, son of good family!"
Mañjuśrī thought to himself:
"If I were to reply that there are such eyes and ears and that there is something seen and heard, then I would be reckoning them as permanent;
if, on the other hand, I were to say that there are no eyes and no ears, then I would fall into the view of annihilationism."
Those whose conduct involves the view of annihilation or the calculation of permanence do not understand the Dharma.
One who acts in accordance with the Dharma neither holds to annihilation nor calculates permanence.
Being without annihilation and without calculating permanence, there is nothing that arises; where there is nothing that arises, there is no verbal expression.
"For this reason, Mañjuśrī, by remaining silent and without speaking when faced with these difficult questions, he has answered the Buddha.
When these words were spoken, six hundred bodhisattvas attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"Out of respect for you, I have sent you away to dwell on the summit of Mount Cakravāḍa because of three matters in which you are attached and obstructed."
Furthermore, you asked:
"By what causes and conditions does the woman Vimati alone remain and not emerge?
This woman Vimati has entered into the meditative absorption (samādhi) of Universal Moon Stainless Radiance.

The mind is forever free from thought, whether the Buddhas come or do not come, whether they preach the Dharma or do not preach it; one never conceives the notion of a Buddha nor the notion of the Dharma, and being without the notion of self or other, one eliminates all thoughts and delusive imaginings.

Abiding in this samādhi, the woman universally hears the Buddhas preaching the Dharma in the present Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions—countless, myriad, hundreds of thousands of billions of years in number—yet she remains entirely unattached.
Whatever she hears and receives, she explains for the sake of others.

While possessing this female body, she does not go from this land to other Buddha-fields; though she dwells in various lands, she has no notion of "land"; though she abides among the Buddhas, she has no notion of "Buddha"; and when hearing the Dharma being taught, she has no notion of "sutra. She is without the notion of a self and without the notion of others, just as the lunar palace never moves or shifts yet descends to the human world, its radiance shining everywhere so that none fail to see it.
Just as the moonlight shines without regard for distance or proximity, and harbors no such thought as, "I shall illuminate this person, but not that one," so too is this woman:

dwelling in samādhi, she manifests throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds to deliver, liberate, and transform countless sentient beings; yet, while manifesting in all the Buddha-lands, she does not harbor thoughts regarding these sentient beings as she expounds the sūtras.
For one kalpa and even beyond another kalpa, the Buddha praised and extolled the virtues of this woman, Vimati, yet he could not fully express them or reach their ultimate limit.
The meritorious achievements of this woman are inconceivable; they are as magnificent as this!
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
"When the assemblies of the Buddhas convene, are the hundreds of thousands of millions of bodhisattvas from this buddha-field transferred to other realms?"
“Is it as if I have been dismissed?
The Buddha said,
“Be silent for now, Mañjuśrī!”
One must not attempt to measure the noble wisdom of the Tathāgata, nor should one regard the manifestations established by the Tathāgata as being of a uniform nature.
Why is this so? This, Mañjuśrī!
The three thousandfold great thousandfold world-systems were filled with Buddhas, like groves of sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, rice, and hemp; the number of Tathāgatas assembled was as great as this.

In this land, among the assembly of bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, not a single one sees anything other than my single body as a Tathāgata; nor do they hear the various Buddhas preaching the Dharma, but see only my own body proclaiming the transformation of the Way.

Mañjuśrī, observe this: that which is established by the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, involves inconceivable and limitless transformations of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*). His body is subtle and wondrous, filled with all Buddhas, pervading the entire trichiliocosm without exception. While the assembly of bodhisattvas perceives each Tathāgata with their eye of the Way (*dharma-cakṣus*), how much more so for others; as for those who wish to see him [in such a way], it has never been possible.

The devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, and others—both human and non-human—who roam this trichiliocosm, moving about, coming and going, standing, sitting, reclining, or sleeping, do so with tranquil composure and dignified decorum; their conduct is perfectly orderly and unimpeded, for the bodies of all Tathāgatas are without limit or obstruction.

"Therefore, Mañjuśrī, you should form this contemplation: all Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body; they possess no physical form or image. The Buddha-body is without outflows (*anāsrava*); all outflows have been exhausted, and thus there is no body. Contemplating it, it has no counterpart; it is without birth and without arising, without being seen and without being heard, without mind and without location. It is also like empty space, devoid of all outflows, without causes, conditions, or faculties, without image and without visibility, and cannot be grasped or held. One may wish to behold empty space, yet it cannot be seen; it is not within the range of the five eyes."
What are the five eyes?
First is the divine eye;
second is the fleshly eye.
The third is the wisdom eye;
the fourth is the dharma eye;
the fifth is the buddha eye.

That which is called "empty space" is merely a provisional name; the body of the Tathāgata is likewise so: it is without outflows, without form, and there is no one who sees it, for it possesses no sense faculties.

There is no seeing of the Tathāgata; the Buddha does not possess five eyes. The "Tathāgata" and "Ultimate Reality" (tattva) are merely provisional names, and thus there is nothing to which they correspond. Mañjuśrī!

Observe this assembly of Tathāgatas: their supernormal powers and transformations are such that their bodies are like empty space, yet they nevertheless manifest at appropriate times physical bodies endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.
“Mañjuśrī! Those bodies of the Tathāgatas that were seen just now were all moved by the power established through the majestic spiritual authority of the Buddhas. Why is this so?
"Because of the sake of benevolent ones, you shall manifest the infinitely profound and wondrous teaching of the Dharma.
At that time, the bodhisattvas assembled in that buddha-field raised their voices in unison and praised him, saying:
"How truly unprecedented! How marvelous and joyful! The majestic spiritual transformations of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are as sublime as this!"
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions have all come to this assembly, filling the Buddha-fields.
We Bodhisattvas do not see a single Buddha, nor do we recall their forms or voices; who comes and who goes? What is being explained or analyzed regarding the meaning of the sutras?
We see only this one Honored Tathāgata together.
We pray, O Great Sage!

Now that we behold the unsurpassed noble wisdom of the Mahāyāna, for the sake of each and every person, we would rather endure being boiled in the hells throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges while practicing the bodhisattva path; we must not abandon such peerless wisdom.
Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha Tathāgata Devendra:
"How long has it been since this woman first resolved her mind upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and true path?
Her practice is so serene and her vows so lofty; how is it that her concentration is such as this?"
The Buddha said:

"Since first generating the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment, an incalculable time has passed. Diligent and harboring faith, always free from negligence, he has fulfilled the path of the Buddhas through giving, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, single-minded concentration, and wisdom. His practice is complete, and he follows the teachings of all the Buddhas."
"In past buddhas she has planted many roots of virtue and made offerings to countless billions of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Great Holy Ones. Mañjuśrī!
Now this woman shall arise from samādhi; you may question her as to how long it has been since she first resolved her mind upon the Way."
"You shall be dismissed upon seeing her.

Thereupon, having heard the Buddha’s command, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat and went to where the girl was. With a sincere heart, he snapped his fingers and raised a great sound, wishing to cause the girl to arise; however, she remained unmoved within her samādhi of profound stillness.

Mañjuśrī then manifested infinite bodies just as they appeared, raising his fingers even higher; the sound of his snapping fingers was heard throughout countless worlds in the ten directions, yet the woman remained tranquil and did not arise from her meditative concentration.

At that time, Mañjuśrī, remaining in his physical form, entered into samādhi and manifested great supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*). All sentient beings within the trichiliocosm—humans of the world, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis—saw all their musical instruments sound spontaneously without being struck. Furthermore, he miraculously created ten thousand kinds of musical performances, including lutes, harps, zithers, and flutes, which simultaneously produced soft sounds, clear and elegant tones, and plaintive melodies. Each instrument proclaimed countless resonances that reached throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, yet they were unable to cause the maiden to rise from her samādhi.
At that time, in the presence of the Buddhas currently residing throughout the ten directions, each of their attendant monks asked his respective Buddha:
"For what reason today do these countless and immeasurable great musical sounds, with such pure and harmonious tones, resound throughout all the Buddha-fields?"
Their voices were soft and gentle; there was no one who did not rejoice at their sorrowful melodies.
At that time, each of the Buddhas said to his attendant: "Noble son!..."

In the world-system Samantaprabhā, there is the Tathāgata Devarāja; in that land there is a woman named Vimati who sits to the right of the Buddha, having entered the meditative absorption of Samantacandrarajovimalaprabhā.

There is a bodhisattva named Mañjuśrī, who has donned the armor of great virtue and transcended the stage of non-retrogression; desiring to cause this woman to awaken from her samādhi, he has moved her in such a manner.

The various people of the world, devas, nāgas, spirits, gandharvas, and others, produced hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of musical instruments; all these manifested musical instruments played spontaneously of their own accord, likewise sounding without being struck, desiring to cause this woman to arise from her samādhi, yet they were unable to rouse her.
"For this reason, great music pervades the world.
The attendant addressed the Buddha:

"It is truly unprecedented and beyond compare; the samādhi of this woman is so profoundly still and majestic that it cannot be measured. Even with such various kinds of harmonious musical melodies, the woman continues in her samādhi without arising from it."
The Buddhas replied, "It is as these sons of noble family have said; this girl’s samādhi is inconceivable.

When these words were spoken, immeasurable and incalculable multitudes of sentient beings from the ten directions all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment, each singing in praise:

“May we attain such a samādhi of tranquil concentration as this girl has, and may we achieve the infinite transformations of supernormal power and the penetrating mastery of holy penetration, just like Mañjuśrī.”

At that time, Mañjuśrī again entered a samādhi corresponding to his form, transforming the trichiliocosm so that Sumeru, the king of mountains, the Snowy Mountains, the Black Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Mahāmucilinda, the Iron Ring Mountains, and the Great Iron Ring Mountains all collided with one another, unable to remain stable.
It was like a valiant warrior clapping his two palms together with great force, or like a great thunderclap whose sound resounds so freely that there is no one who does not hear it.

Mount Sumeru, the Iron Encircling Mountains, and all other mountains shook against one another in succession until each collapsed; these mountains fell to the ground in terrifying forms, and the sound was most piteous. Furthermore, that great sound was heard throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds, yet the woman’s samādhi remained unmoved and undisturbed.

At that time, Mañjuśrī did not approach the woman; instead, using skillful means, he took her by both hands and attempted to make her rise from her seat. He thereby caused all Buddha-fields in the lower direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to tremble, yet he could not move the woman even as much as a hair’s breadth, nor could he cause her to emerge from her samādhi.

Furthermore, he exerted all his power and attempted to lift her up; yet the Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were all uprooted and turned upside down, and still he could not cause the woman to arise from her samādhi.

Mañjuśrī severed the ground where the girl was sitting and, lifting it up with his right palm, tossed it to the Brahma Heaven; yet even as she sat upon the ground in the Brahma Heaven, he could not cause her to arise from her samādhi.

Then Mañjuśrī again took the girl’s body from the Brahma heaven, placed it upon his right palm, and traveled past as many Buddha-fields in the eastern direction as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; he did likewise for the southern, western, northern, four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, each reaching as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.

In the lands of the ten directions, all manner of musical instruments resounded; mountains collapsed with a terrifying roar, and celestial flowers rained down. The resonance was so vast and sublime that it defied all analogy, yet it could not cause the woman to arise from her samādhi.

At that time, Mañjuśrī lifted the woman and cast her throughout the ten directions, yet he could not awaken her; he then returned her to her original place and, with palms joined, stepped forward and addressed the Tathāgata Deva-rāja:
"Indeed, Great Sage!..."

The practices of these bodhisattvas are unprecedented, beyond reach, and inconceivable to thought or measurement. I am able to cause all vessels to transform and dwell in space, standing, moving about, walking, coming and going, and conversing; now manifesting infinite supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), they produce transformations and stir up great sounds, shattering Mount Sumeru and the Iron Ring Mountains, uprooting buddha-fields and shifting the worlds of the ten directions, yet they can never cause them to arise from their samādhi.

I shall humbly pay homage to you, as well as to the rest of the assembly of great bodhisattvas—sons of noble family or daughters of noble family who have first resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, whether they have already achieved it, are in the process of achieving it, or are just beginning their studies—and those who aspire to and delight in such infinite, great wisdom should likewise take refuge in it.
Why is this? Because the conduct of a bodhisattva is beyond comparison.

Mañjuśrī took the woman Vimilāprabhā to the buddha-fields of the ten directions and traveled back and forth throughout them; yet the sounds he produced could not cause the woman to arise from her samādhi.

At that time, he transformed and enlightened countless sentient beings throughout the ten directions, causing them to resolve upon the Way, and led immeasurable people to establish the roots of manifold virtues.
The Tathāgata Tianwang replied to Mañjuśrī, saying:

"It is truly as you have said; the armor of virtue donned by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas is inconceivable, beyond the reach of knowledge for all Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, let alone what ordinary folk can attain."
It is as if the trichiliocosm were to become a great drum; the drums of other distinct worlds would likewise be as large as that one, immeasurable in their breadth and length.

At that time, a great man suddenly appeared; his body was immense, as vast as the trichiliocosm, and he raised a great drumstick as large as a thousand worlds. He then struck this great drum before the woman for an entire kalpa, or even longer than a kalpa, yet he could not cause the sound to reach her ears, much less cause her to arise from samādhi—such a thing had never occurred.
“Mañjuśrī! If you wish to know this girl’s samādhi, it is tranquil, settled, and peaceful, never wavering or shifting; such is the wisdom of the Way, its majestic power being limitless.
Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha:
"Who is capable of moving this woman and causing her to arise from samādhi?
The Buddha replied to Mañjuśrī:
"Only a Tathāgata can cause her to arise; furthermore, there is a bodhisattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin who can also cause her to arise."
As soon as the Buddha had formed this thought, the merit and virtue of this son of noble family caused the trichiliocosm to shake in six ways.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva by the name of King Lamp-Light (Dīpamkara-rāja) standing beside the Buddha Tathāgata; serving as the Buddha’s attendant, he stepped forward and asked the Buddha:
"By what causes and conditions does the earth now shake so violently?"
The Buddha told his attendant:

“Because of the praise just now for the name of the Bodhisattva Abandoning All Skandha-Coverings, this trichiliocosm shook with a great trembling; furthermore, in whatever directions the Tathāgatas in the various Buddha-fields of other quarters praised this name, the lands there likewise shook in six ways.”

At that time, all the bodhisattvas in the assembly were filled with a sense of longing and emptiness, desiring to see where the Bodhisattva Abandoning All Veils (Sarvāvaraṇaprahāṇa) was; Mañjuśrī was likewise the same.
Mañjuśrī, perceiving the thoughts in the minds of the bodhisattvas and also out of his own reverence and delight, desired to cause the woman to arise; he addressed the Buddha, the King of Heaven:
"Excellent!..."
World-Honored One!

We pray that you will graciously manifest your majestic radiance; for all those gathered here harbor a thirsting longing and desire to behold the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Abandoner of All Shrouds and Obstructions.

The Tathāgata, out of universal compassion, manifested only his supreme and holy path of divine power (*ṛddhi*), causing the son of noble family to travel to this buddha-field to expound the profound Dharma. When the bodhisattvas heard it, they were thereby enabled to study the meaning of ultimate truth; furthermore, he caused the daughter to arise from samādhi and revealed what she had not yet attained.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King of Lamp-Light asked the Buddha Heavenly King:
"In which direction and in which buddha-field does that son of good family reside?"
"What is the name of the Tathāgata in that land? That Buddha replied:

"Below this world, past as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, there is a realm named Kintaka-dhvaja. The Buddha there is named Siṃha-gaja-śikhara-nardita Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma."

That buddha-field consists entirely of bodhisattvas who have donned inconceivable armor of great virtue; they completely fill that buddha-field, and the Tathāgata constantly proclaims the wheel of non-retrogression.
"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Abandoning All Obscurations (*Sarvāvaraṇaprahāṇa*) roams in that land.

While the Tathāgata King of Devas (*Devendra*) sat majestically upon his throne, from the big toe of his right foot he emanated a golden light; this light was named "Inviting All Bodhisattvas. As soon as he emitted this radiance, it illuminated Buddha-fields equal in number to the sands of the Ganges in the regions below.
That radiance shone brilliantly, encircling the body of the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin seven times before vanishing into the crown of his head.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin thought to himself:
"For what reason now does this soft, pure, harmonious, and infinite radiance circle me seven times and vanish into my crown?"
He immediately understood that the Tathāgata Heavenly King (Devarāja) wished to see him.
He then proceeded to the place where the Tathāgata Lion-Eagle-Elephant-Crested-Lion’s-Roar (Siṃha-śikhara-hastin-śikhararava-nardita) was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to go to the world of Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā) in the upward direction to visit the Buddha Heavenly King; that Tathāgata there now desires to see me."
The Buddha said,
“Go, son of good family!”
"You should know that this is the time.

Then, in the presence of the Tathāgata Siṃha-garuḍa-hasti-śikhara-nirghoṣa, there was a bodhisattva named Saṃghārthavighuṣṭa who served as the Buddha’s attendant. He came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to see the world Samantaprabhā and the Tathāgata Devendrarāja."
When the Lion-Eagle-Elephant-Crested Roar reached the Perfectly Awakened One, he was pleased and approved.

Immediately, he emitted a light from the mark between his eyebrows, which illuminated Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the zenith, pervading the Universal Radiance Realm. There, everyone together beheld from afar the Tathāgata Heavenly King, surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas and retinues, as he preached the sutra.

The Buddha’s body alone was manifest like a mountain of purple gold; his radiance surpassed the brilliance of the sun and moon. Just as one with clear vision perceives a person’s face with complete clarity and distinction, so too did the entire assembly perceive the Buddha Tianshou, as well as all the bodhisattvas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Abandoning All Obscurations, together with five hundred thousand bodhisattvas, vanished from that buddha-field and, in the mere blink of an eye, arrived at the realm of Universal Radiance where they were in the presence of the Buddha Heavenly King.

Having cast off all hindrances and obscurations, together with the various bodhisattvas, he bared his right shoulder, prostrated before the Buddha Deva-rāja, and having circumambulated him three times, withdrew to stand in the void.

At that time, the bodhisattvas, having attained the samādhi of "Comprehending All Bodies," cast off all hindrances and obscurations; they immediately beheld auspicious omens corresponding to their own forms. Displaying their supernormal powers, they scattered flowers from the sky like falling rain. These flowers were dispersed before, behind, to the left, and to the right of the Tathāgata Heavenly King. These flowers emitted sounds proclaiming subtle and wondrous meanings:
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Lion-Eagle-Elephant-Crest Roar sends his respectful greetings:
Are you free from ailment? Is your physical well-being secure? Is your movement light and agile? Is your strength at ease?"
At that time, the assembly marveled at what had never occurred before:
"By whose majestic power have these flowers produced such gentle sounds to proclaim their reverent intent?
Mañjuśrī then questioned the Buddha Tathāgata Devendra.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
By whose holy intention were these myriad flowers rained down and this subtle, wondrous sound produced?
The Buddha replied to Mañjuśrī:
"The Bodhisattva Abandoning All Shrouds (Sarvāvaraṇaprahāṇa) has manifested a majestic transformation.
He then asked the World-Honored One: "Where is he now?"
The Buddha said:
"He was in the air above, having attained the samādhi of the 'Comprehension of All Bodies' (sarvakāyavibhakti).
He asked again:
"Why do the assembly of bodhisattvas not appear?
The Buddha said,
"The spiritual power of the Bodhisattva Abandoning All Obscurations (Sarvāvaraṇaprahāṇa) prevents them from appearing."
Mañjuśrī thought to himself:
"I shall, by means of this samādhi-samāpatti, seek out where these bodhisattvas reside.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin immediately knew of this; he then made his form vanish and addressed Mañjuśrī:
"What do you think? Is there only this one samādhi of comprehending all bodies?
Do not hold such a view; the number of samādhis for comprehending all bodies is beyond measure."
The samādhi you have just entered is like but a single drop within the great ocean.
The various samādhis and meditative attainments of my body, as I sit and arise from them, are beyond all measure; the names of those you have cultivated thus far have never been heard before.
Mañjuśrī further thought to himself:
"I should rather contemplate the sublime practices I cultivated in my past lives; by means of these, I shall surely attain this samādhi."
Immediately, according to his thought, it was just as he had envisioned; in the time of a single finger-snap, he attained all the samādhis.
Then, the Buddha Tathāgata Devendra addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas:
"O sons of noble family!..."

All together observe this karma of diligence, which brings about a state of extraordinary and transcendent significance; it is only after hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas of diligent practice and accumulation of merit that other bodhisattvas attain this samādhi.
"Now, Mañjuśrī, in the mere twinkling of an eye, you can manifest them all.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, the Heavenly King:
"Please deign to manifest them, for these members of the assembly of bodhisattvas, both noble men and women, all wish to see them."
Having cast off all hindrances and obscurations along with the other bodhisattvas, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and immediately vanished from his body.
He then asked Mañjuśrī, “Can we see one another?”
He replied, “I do not see them.
The Tathāgata Devendra addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin:
"I have ventured to come to this assembly desiring to see you all; I shall now manifest my own body.

Upon these words, the bodhisattvas immediately accepted the instruction and, together with the assembly of true beings (*samyaksattva*) and bodhisattvas, arose from samādhi. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and withdrew to one side. There, in accordance with their original vows, they manifested as lotus flowers and sat upon them.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī said to the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin:
"Arouse this woman from her samādhi. He replied:
"Stop! The realm of empty space possesses no samādhi, nor does it arise; furthermore, empty space cannot be moved.
When Mañjuśrī spoke those words just now, he caused this woman to rise from samādhi. Was she made to emerge from concentration by means of her name?"
Is it by means of form?
Or is it by means of consciousness?
When one contemplates that form is of its own nature, it does not constitute samādhi; it is neither a correct reception nor an arising.
That consciousness is spontaneous; it does not undergo meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), nor does it arise.
All phenomena (*dharma*) likewise lack intrinsic purity; they neither undergo meditative absorption nor do they arise.
"Now, what dharma should I bring forth?
If, Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are samādhi,
and I am to cause them to arise, yet there is ultimately no meditative attainment (samāpatti), what is it that could possibly be brought forth?"
"Why is this so? Because all dharmas are entirely without arising or establishment, and likewise without existence or cessation.
Thus spoke the Tathāgata Devendra to Apagataskandhāvaraṇa.
“You, son of good family, have caused this woman to arise from samādhi. He addressed the Buddha, saying: “I am not fit to proclaim my own merits before the Tathāgata;

it is fitting that I remain concealed. It is the True Tathāgata who should cause this woman to arise from samādhi. Even if I were capable of causing this woman to rise from samādhi, the Tathāgata, the Truly Realized One, universally understands all dharmas with unimpeded wisdom; he preaches the Dharma according to the occasion without anything being obstructed. He should cause the woman to arise from samādhi, so that upon seeing the divine power of the Buddha-way, all may rejoice and resolve upon the Great Mind.”
At that time, the Buddha, King of Devas, entered the meditative absorption of the Samādhi of Arousing Concentration.

Having entered this concentration, at that very moment, all the devas, nāgas, spirits, and people of the world in that trichiliocosm, as well as the assembly of bodhisattvas who were themselves in meditative absorption, and that woman, all arose from their concentration.
As he rose from his seat, the ten directions immediately shook in six ways, and all [the assemblies] leaped upward and stayed suspended in mid-air.
At that moment, countless hundreds of thousands of devas came to the assembly.
The women remained in mid-air, raining down blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses as an offering to the Tathāgata.
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked the girl Viśeṣamati:
“This unprecedented and tranquil practice, and the samādhi you have attained, are beyond reach.”
The girl replied, "Mañjuśrī,
wait! Please stop!"
Do not harbor deluded thoughts; in the samādhi of stillness, there is forever nothing to be attained. Why is this?

For the wisdom of the path cultivated by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is without anything to be acquired. Whoever has something to acquire has something to lose. All dharmas are tranquil, silent, and quiescent; that which is quiescent has nothing further to be quiescent. Furthermore, that quiescence is not a state of samādhi; there is no meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), nor is there any arising from it.
Mañjuśrī replied: "It is truly as your words say;

your eternal stability is most extraordinary. Were it not for this subtle and unsurpassed samādhi, there would be something attained; yet you give rise to vast and infinite sounds without them arising!"
The woman asked again:
"In that dharma-realm, can there be samādhi or even the arising from it? Mañjuśrī replied:
"No," she replied. The woman asked again:
"Can one who is not in samādhi be caused to arise from it?"
"Is there perhaps some form, likeness, or appearance? Mañjuśrī replied,
"If there were no form, likeness, or appearance, who would be in samādhi?"
The girl replied:
“That all phenomena are fundamentally pure is samādhi; there is no further concentration of the mind, nor is anything produced. Therefore, all phenomena are entirely like echoes.”
"For example, can the various kinds of music enjoyed by the devas and the people of the world produce their respective exquisite sounds?
She replied, "It is as my sister says."
He asked again:
"Does that realm of empty space harbor such a thought?
Does it think to produce these various kinds of musical performances and harmonious, sorrowful melodies?"
He replied: "No, Mañjuśrī. For this reason," he said.
"All dharmas are equal to empty space; who hears that sound?
Only if there is auditory consciousness can one hear sound. Mañjuśrī asked:
"Do you have no ears, woman?
Why do you not hear?
The woman remained silent and spoke no word.
Mañjuśrī questioned her again, repeating this up to three times, but the girl remained silent and did not reply.
The girl then answered:
“It is not that I have not heard.”
He asked again,
"Why do you remain silent? The girl replied:
"Always there is nothing to be attained.
The girl Liyi asked Mañjuśrī again:
"It is just as you say, Mañjuśrī!"

A great turbulent wind arises and spreads everywhere, entering into the great trees; no one can see what its appearance or nature is. The wind has no conceptual thought, and the trees have no thoughts; the wind does not think:
"It is I who enter the great trees and cause them to shake."
The tree, likewise, does not think:
"The wind enters my body.
In this same way, the Bodhisattva constantly practices the wisdom of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, completely eliminating all conceptualizations, and does not think to himself:
"I am in samādhi," nor does he think,
"I shall arise from samādhi."
"Why is this so? Because all dharmas are fundamentally pure. Mañjuśrī said:
"Sister! You should descend from the void and stand before the Tathāgata before speaking of this matter.
The woman replied:
"I establish my own practice and do not employ the practices of others.
Mañjuśrī asked again,
"What is meant by 'one's own practice'?"
The girl replied: "All sentient beings exist because of space. Why is this so? Because..."

All classes of sentient beings rely entirely upon empty space as they circulate and come and go; their dwellings, occupations, clothing, food, and drink, and all that they undertake and create, do not depart from empty space.
"Therefore, sentient beings naturally roam in space; all dharmas are sealed by the vision of emptiness.
At that time, the woman immediately descended from the void and withdrew to sit upon a lotus flower to one side, neither prostrating to the Tathāgata nor offering any words of thanks.
Mañjuśrī asked, "Gopā,
daughter of Māra, are you so excessively arrogant that you do not maintain a respectful demeanor, nor do you pay homage to the Tathāgata,
but instead sit here in silence? The girl replied:
"It is truly as the Tathāgata has said; I am indeed without reverence.
Why is this? Because there is nothing performed, yet there is also nothing unperformed."
"What do you think?
Can that which is fundamentally non-existent be venerated? He replied:
"No," the girl replied, "for this reason, the Buddha cannot be venerated."
"Why is this? If one calculates the primordial non-existence and the Honored Tathāgata, there are no two; they should be viewed with equanimity.
He then asked Mañjuśrī again:
“Do you see the Tathāgata? Mañjuśrī replied,
“I regard him with equanimity.”
He asked again:
"By what means do you contemplate? Mañjuśrī replied:
"Because they are without origin and so forth, one observes them with equanimity;
because they are without form or image, one observes them with equanimity.
My right observation is such that it is equal in this way."
The girl asked again:
"In such contemplations as these, what is it that one sees? He replied:
"One who observes in this way sees nothing.
The woman asked again:
"Is it that one sees nothing with the fleshly eye?"
He replied: "Neither by the fleshly eye, nor by the divine eye. Why is this so?"
"The eye is neither produced nor arisen; it is like a magical illusion, neither existent nor non-existent, and it should not be described as having the nature of existence or non-existence.
Mañjuśrī asked the girl, "For what reason do you not transform your female body now?"
The girl replied: "Mañjuśrī, please stop!
Do not harbor such deluded thoughts.
For one who possesses the contemplative insight and has realized all dharmas, could there be male or female?"
He replied, “There is none. He asked again:
"If one calculates regarding form (rūpa), are there males and females?
He replied, "There are not."
“Are there male or female in feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness? He replied, “There are not.”
“Do earth, water, fire, and wind possess male or female? He replied, “They do not.”
“Space is vast and open, without boundaries; no location can be perceived—could there be men or women therein? He replied, “No.”
He asked Mañjuśrī again:
"Regarding the written words you have spoken, do they have a beginning or an end, a location, or can they be categorized as male or female? He replied:
“There is none,” his daughter replied.
“Why did you speak those words just now?”
"Why do you not now transform your female body? [The Bodhisattva replied:
"If I were already to perceive myself as having attained the state of a woman and as seeing both men and women, then I would cast off this female form and receive a male body."
I do not perceive a woman nor do I see a man; for what reason, then, would one abandon the female form to become a male?

When one calculates the nature of all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is neither conjunction nor dispersion, neither origin nor ultimate limit. They are empty, still, and like space, without conjunction or dispersion. Since all phenomena are entirely like space, by what cause could a female form be transformed into a male?
"Why is this? Because this is the foremost teaching proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
He then asked the woman:

"The eye has neither male nor female; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind likewise have neither male nor female. If all phenomena (dharmas) are without male or female, then being neither joined nor dispersed, they are without male or female."
Mañjuśrī again asked the girl,
"How long has it been since you first resolved to attain the Way? The girl replied:
"Just as a phantom created by a magician exists through the persistence of consciousness, so too is it with me in my resolve for the Way, whether far or near. Why is this? Because..."
All dharmas are entirely like illusions and transformations.
Previously, Mañjuśrī posed this question:
"How long has it been since this girl first resolved her mind upon the Way?"
Such an awakening is not a principle that can be questioned.
Why is this? That which is unarisen cannot be made to arise; nor can one find a location for the mind. Since it has no location, that which is unarisen neither arises nor ceases.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
“If one acts in this manner, what kind of wisdom should one follow and accord with?
The girl replied:
"Non-hearing and non-speaking are what accord with wisdom.
He asked again: "What is meant by 'accordance'?"
The girl replied, "That which is unarisen is what accords with reality.
He questioned the girl again:
“How long has it been since you attained the patience regarding dharmas?
He replied, “None at all.”
He asked again:
"Has the girl attained the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)? She replied:
"No. He asked again: "For what reason?"

He replied: "That which is unarisen is unattainable; for this reason, one does not attain the patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti), nor does one reach the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattikadharmakṣānti)."
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Daughter, perceiving what meaning have you donned the armor of the great vow and resolved upon the mind of enlightenment? The girl replied:
"Because all sentient beings are not subject to extinction, for this reason the Bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of enlightenment and cultivates the armor of the great vows.
He asked again:
"For what reason?"
He replied: "Because all sentient beings and all phenomena are utterly extinguished. Why is this so?"
Mañjuśrī! All the Buddhas of the past, the perfectly awakened ones, did not deliver sentient beings; likewise, those of the future and the present have nothing to deliver. Why is this so?
"All sentient beings emerge from the void.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"For what cause does the Buddha appear in the world?"
He replied: "It is because he wishes to bring about the state of non-creation and non-action that he has appeared in the world. Why is this so? Because..."
"One who practices in accordance with this neither acts nor refrains from acting.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"For what reason does one leave the household life, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu?"
The girl replied,
"It is because I wish to fulfill the five heinous crimes.
He asked again:
"Who would believe such words as these?
He replied, "Only those who do not give rise to [conceptualization], who have nothing that arises, and who harbor nothing, will believe this."
He asked again,
"By what means do you have faith and joy? He replied:
"To have nothing to speak of is called 'faithful delight.
He asked again:
"If one does not delight in liberation, what fetters and obstructions are there?"
He replied, "Those who do not delight in liberation find liberation to be a fetter and an obstruction. Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is most unprecedented, difficult to equal, and truly beyond compare; the eloquence you have displayed is entirely unimpeded.
The girl replied, "Cease!
[Do not speak thus]."
Mañjuśrī! Do not engage in such contrary conduct.
Now that you stand before this assembly, which is obstructed and shrouded in darkness, for what reason do you extol the principle of non-obstruction?
He asked again:
"Is there no teaching? He replied:
"There is no speaking; therefore, my body speaks without obstruction.
He asked again:
"Does the vast expanse of empty space possess eloquence?"
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"What is meant by 'eloquence'? The girl replied:
"That which is unarisen is called eloquence.
He asked again,
"What is meant by 'unarisen'?"
He replied: "That which is called 'non-arising' refers to following and practicing in accordance with the dharma-realm; that the primordial limit has no basis—this is what is meant by 'practice.
He then asked Mañjuśrī again:
"It is that which is not practiced that constitutes true practice.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'not practicing'?"
He replied: "To act within the three realms while having no place of action, to exist within the three realms while having no location—this is to have no attachment whatsoever in all that one does."
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"After how long will you, daughter, attain supreme perfect enlightenment? The girl replied:
"Just as the Tathāgata, the Celestial King Buddha, attained supreme perfect enlightenment, so shall I likewise.
What do you think, O worthy one?
Can the Way be realized?"
"Have you attained a dwelling place?
Mañjuśrī remained silent at that time.
The girl spoke again to Mañjuśrī:
"It would be appropriate to speak at this time; should it not be so?
Mañjuśrī replied, "The Way is beyond verbal expression; for this reason, I do not know how to speak."
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed the Celestial King Buddha:
"It is truly unprecedented,
O God among Gods!"

This woman’s wisdom and clarity are inconceivable; her extraordinary virtues are beyond comparison. Now that what she has proclaimed is so majestic, it is evident how long she has been cultivating the aspiration for the Way, and in the future she shall likewise achieve supreme perfect enlightenment.
"What is the name of that buddha-field?
What is the designation of the Buddha's name? The Buddha said:

“Before you, O Benevolent One, ninety-six billion hundred thousand koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, after having practiced the path for as many kalpas, Mañjuśrī subsequently gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment.”
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"From which Buddha did this girl originally resolve her mind toward the Way?
The Buddha said:

"From the time he first resolved his mind on the Way under the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava, the virtue and purity of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava’s land have been beyond measure. Even if one were to praise them for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, one could not exhaustively describe the excellence and joy of that buddha-field's meritorious achievements; it was by following that Buddha that he first resolved his mind on the Way."
He asked again:
"In her previous life, was this woman a female? He replied:
"No. At that time, this woman became a wheel-turning monarch named Asaṃkhyeya.
Mañjuśrī, you should know that she was neither a woman nor a man."

Why is this? Because he has already attained the Illusion-like Samādhi (māyopama-samādhi), whereby he is able to manifest whatever he desires, appearing through transformations according to the occasion.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

This woman shall further, for as many hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas as there are particles of dust in the earth of a trichiliocosm, or particles upon the flowers and fruits thereof, attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path and achieve supreme perfect enlightenment. She shall be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, and World-Honored One. Within her land of great merit and virtue, the splendor and purity of its adornments shall be exactly like those of the land of the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava; this woman’s realm shall likewise be equal, without any difference.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, the Heavenly King:
“Mañjuśrī has brought great benefit, for he contemplates all dharmas of the past and the future.”
Mañjuśrī replied: "It is truly as you have said;
that which can benefit others is inexhaustible, because the dharma-realm itself is inexhaustible."
The Tathāgata Devendra said to Mañjuśrī, “Virtuous One!
Do not engage in a discourse on eloquence together with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Abandoner of All Skandha-Coverings.”
Why is this? The eloquence attained by this son of good family is inconceivable.
As for the samādhis and meditative attainments he has reached—having cast aside all hindrances and coverings—and whatever he establishes, you, O virtuous one, cannot equal them.
"What are the names and titles of his samādhis?
At that time, the newly initiated bodhisattvas in the assembly each thought to themselves:
"He has cast off all veils and hindrances beyond reach; he is universally peerless, practicing the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
The Tathāgata Heavenly King, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those newly initiated practitioners, addressed the Bodhisattva Well-Tamed: "Noble son!

Suppose all the people of the trichiliocosm were to become a single courageous being as valiant as Mañjuśrī; even if one calculated all such beings, they would not be able to attain this samādhi to the extent of a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten-thousandfold, or a billionfold. Even throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they would not reach the level of the samādhi-concentration attained by this woman."

“Mañjuśrī is unable even to know his name. Even if all the sentient beings dwelling throughout the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system were to attain concentration and wisdom equal to that of the daughter Vimukti-mati, they would all be unable to match the power of samādhi and noble wisdom attained by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin; it would not be a hundred-thousand-billionth part of it, nor could any analogy be made.”

They cannot fathom or know the power that arises from the Bodhisattva Abandoning All Shrouds (Sarvāvaraṇaprahīṇa). Even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions were to attain concentration and wisdom equal to the noble wisdom of the Bodhisattva Abandoning All Shrouds, it would not equal the transformative teachings manifested by the Tathāgata’s every lifting and placing of his feet, his movements and comings and goings. The noble wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; its majesty is such that it is beyond all comparison.

At that time, the Buddha praised the wisdom and virtue of these Buddhas, and seventy-two thousand people all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment. With one voice and in unison, they each exclaimed in praise:
"May we ourselves also attain the noble wisdom, just as these [Buddhas] do."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Well-Tamed:

“This woman Vimilā originally exhorted Mañjuśrī to resolve upon the path to enlightenment. Just as with Mañjuśrī, so it is in the worlds of the eastern direction, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—all have been transformed by this woman.”
"Furthermore, son of good family!

When the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Abandoner of All Skandha-Coverings exhorted the woman Vimati to resolve upon the path, it was likewise so for as many beings as there are sands in the Ganges throughout the eight directions and the zenith and nadir."
Those whom I have transformed and enlightened, such as the maiden Vimilāprabhā and others, were no different from one another.

Now that I have attained the Way of the Buddha here and am turning the wheel of Dharma, it was originally due to this son of good family who exhorted me and caused me to resolve upon the mind of enlightenment.

Even reaching back to the distant past, when Buddhas such as Sumerudhvaja were in the world teaching and transforming beings like us; and even now, throughout the ten directions, there are Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, some currently present and others who have entered parinirvāṇa beyond measure—all of whom we see transforming and enlightening others.

As these words were spoken, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; birds and beasts cried out piteously toward one another, rejoicing that they had encountered the Buddha, the Sage; those in the hells and the realm of hungry ghosts all attained liberation, their hearts filled with joy as if seeing light in the darkness; and the pearl ornaments on the women’s arms jingled against one another.
At that time, there was no one who did not rejoice.

When this Dharma was being taught, the gods and humans of the ninety-two *koṭis* in the world-system of Samantaprabhā all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Thereupon, throughout this world, by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all heard this Dharma and joined together in encouragement and support, feeling immeasurable joy and celebration on their behalf.

Maitreya Bodhisattva also received this Dharma and increased his reverence; within this Buddha-land, sixty-four billion devas and humans who heard this Dharma all resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Furthermore, seventy thousand people all attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Fourteen thousand bhikṣus attained liberation of mind and were freed from outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*); five hundred bhikṣuṇīs also attained liberation of mind; and twenty-six thousand people of the world became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur viśuddham*).
Thereupon, Śākyamuni Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva:

"Virtuous One, you should receive this essential core of the sūtra. In the future final age, there will be few who have faith; therefore, entrust it solely to you so that it may be widely disseminated."
Maitreya addressed the Buddha:
“I shall indeed accept it as the Holy One has instructed; I dare not disobey your command.
As for this sutra, wherever it may be circulated in future ages, the merit of those who receive and uphold it will be immeasurable.”

If there are bodhisattvas who make offerings to all the Buddhas of the past who have entered parinirvāṇa, as well as to the infinite holy ones currently manifesting in the ten directions, and to all those who have resolved their minds, established their wills, and are studying the Way—whether they are currently training or yet to train—they cause them all to endure for a long time.

If there were a single person among all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who, in a future age, were to provide offerings to this entire assembly of Tathāgatas—bestowing all manner of peace and security upon all Buddhas of the past, future, and present, honoring them equally and without distinction—would not their merit be great?
Maitreya addressed the Buddha:
“It is many, World-Honored One!
Upon hearing this parable, my mind was bewildered and I could not discern its direction; its number is vast and immeasurable, and the merit is limitless.”
The Buddha said:

"If there is a bodhisattva who receives this sutra, upholds, recites, and reads it, and explains it to others, such that another person hears it even once and rejoices with faith, their merit shall be greater than that of one who makes offerings to all the Buddhas."
The Buddha said to Maitreya:

"Whether I am currently present or have entered parinirvāṇa, if there should be a woman who hears the name and virtuous renown of the maiden Liyi, the title of the Bodhisattva Qizhuyingai, the name of the Tathāgata Tianwang, and this sutra; by virtue of hearing the names, virtues, and transformations described in this sutra, she shall, at the end of this single lifetime, cast off her female body and become a man, swiftly attaining the unsurpassed, perfect, and true Way, and becoming a Most Perfectly Awakened One."

Until he attains Buddhahood, in every lifetime throughout his births, he shall always encounter an age in which a Buddha appears; he shall forever abandon the eight difficulties and various states of distress and lack of leisure; he shall always possess the knowledge of past lives and attain *dhāraṇī*; his body shall be adorned with the thirty-two marks; wherever he dwells or travels, he shall no longer enter a womb but shall always undergo miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).

Why is this? Because the majestic power and spiritual authority of these great bodhisattvas are vast and immeasurable; if any woman hears their names, she too shall subsequently attain such meritorious achievements.

When the Buddha had spoken thus, Maitreya Bodhisattva, the devas, humans, and asuras, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with joy; they bowed their heads in prostration and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sūtra on the Essential Assembly of All Buddhas, Scroll II.
